title: Join-table relationships lack cascade -> db.delete(parent) raises AssertionError and deletes nothing (breaks DELETE /api/pools/{id} and ops.delete_node)

corrected_summary: Node.pool_memberships (models.py:253), Pool.node_memberships (282) and Pool.group_access (283) are plain relationships with no cascade/passive_deletes, so deleting the parent makes SQLAlchemy try to NULL a column that is half of the child's composite primary key; the flush aborts with a bare AssertionError, nothing is deleted, and the route returns 500. Reachable via DELETE /api/pools/{id} (pool with any member node or any group grant) and DELETE /api/nodes/{id} (any pooled node). The Group cases the auditor also listed are unreachable — there is no delete_group op and no groups router.
failure_scenario: Admin creates pool P, adds node N (POST /api/pools/{P}/nodes), then DELETE /api/pools/{P} -> pools.py:227 `await db.delete(pool)` -> AssertionError "Dependency rule on column 'pools.id' tried to blank-out primary key column 'pool_node_memberships.pool_id'" at flush; no handler maps AssertionError, so the operator gets a 500 and P still exists (verified: pool still present == True). Identically, DELETE /api/nodes/{N} for any node that belongs to a pool -> ops.py:657 -> AssertionError on pool_node_memberships.node_id -> 500, i.e. deregistering a node that is actually in service always fails.

title: Job.step_runs has no cascade over a NOT NULL FK -> DELETE /api/jobs/{id} 500s for any job that ran a step
refutation_attempt: Reproduced the exact route body on a job with one step_run and no artifacts (/tmp/nx_repro2.py): "delete job(step_runs only) RAISED: IntegrityError NOT NULL constraint failed: step_runs.job_id [SQL: UPDATE step_runs SET job_id=? WHERE step_runs.id = ?] [parameters: (None, ...)]", and the job row survives. Dumped Base.metadata: step_runs.job_id nullable=False. Checked for upstream guards: jobs.py:557-597 only checks terminal state, then `await db.delete(job)`; no try/except, no app-level handler. Checked tests: test_jobs_routes.py:537 deletes a job created via ops with no step_runs, so nothing pins this as working. BUT two of the auditor's sub-claims are refuted: Job.artifacts and StorageBackend.artifacts cannot fire in production because no production code ever creates an Artifact row — ops.create_artifact's only caller is StorageManager.upload_artifact (manager.py:262), and `grep -rn upload_artifact packages` shows zero non-test callers; the gem5 results path instead writes a tarball to RESULTS_DIR via PUT /api/jobs/{id}/results (jobs.py:322). So "DELETE /api/storage/backends/{id} 500s once any artifact references it" is unreachable today (I did reproduce it artificially by inserting an artifact by hand).
corrected_summary: Job.step_runs (models.py:497) declares no cascade, so deleting a job emits `UPDATE step_runs SET job_id=NULL`, which SQLite rejects because step_runs.job_id is NOT NULL — DELETE /api/jobs/{id} therefore 500s for every job that ever ran a step. The parallel claims about Job.artifacts (498) and StorageBackend.artifacts (430) are technically true of the mappings but unreachable, since nothing in production creates Artifact rows.
failure_scenario: Any real job (>=1 step) reaches status="completed"; the user clicks Delete -> jobs.py:596 `await db.delete(job)` -> sqlite3.IntegrityError "NOT NULL constraint failed: step_runs.job_id" -> 500 instead of 204, and the job is never removed. Consequence: job history can never be pruned through the API — only the artificial case of a job that dispatched no step can be deleted, which is exactly what the existing test covers.
fix: Add cascade="all, delete-orphan" to Job.step_runs (and Job.artifacts) at models.py:497-498, or delete child rows in the route before db.delete(job). Also fix the jobs.py:592-595 AI Note, which claims "on SQLite (no FK enforcement by default) this succeeds silently" — wrong, because NOT NULL is enforced regardless of PRAGMA foreign_keys.

title: resume_active_jobs() always fails a job resumed at a remote step
refutation_attempt: I looked for any mechanism that would let the re-dispatch succeed or be retried. (1) main.py:186-198 awaits resume_active_jobs inside the lifespan `async with`, before `yield` at line 205 — ASGI does not accept connections until lifespan startup returns, so no agent socket can exist. (2) _execute_remote_step has exactly one placement attempt (runner.py:658-680) and one send attempt (runner.py:733-737); no loop, no sleep, no re-queue anywhere in the module. (3) grepped for a queue sweeper / heartbeat reaper that might re-adopt a failed or queued job later — there is none (the only 'stale' handling is the per-message node status write in ws.py). (4) Ran both branches against an in-memory DB: graceful shutdown (node row already offline from ws.py's finally) gives status='failed' error="No available node for step 'run_command'"; hard crash (node row still online, no live socket) gives status='failed' error='Agent for node h-... not connected'. Also confirmed every test in the resume section of tests/integration/test_runner_resume.py uses {"step": "sleep"}, so the remote case is untested.
corrected_summary: Crash recovery is structurally unable to recover the common case: resume runs before the server accepts connections, and _execute_remote_step fails a step immediately when no node matches or no socket exists, so any job whose current_step is a node-bound step is turned from 'running' into 'failed' at startup instead of being resumed. Note the no-retry half is author-flagged at runner.py:664-668; the resume interaction is not, and resume.py's own docstring assumes re-dispatch works.
failure_scenario: Job J is executing step 0 (run_command) on node N when the server is restarted (a deploy, a uvicorn --reload, or a crash). At next startup resume_active_jobs re-submits J; the task reaches _execute_remote_step within milliseconds, while no agent has reconnected. Graceful restart -> find_node_for_step returns None -> job failed with "No available node for step 'run_command'". Hard crash -> node row still 'online' but send_to_agent returns False -> job failed with "Agent for node <host> not connected". Both reproduced. The same applies to a job merely queued seconds before the restart.
fix: Give the remote path a bounded wait for placement/connectivity (retry 'no eligible node' and 'agent not connected' for ~heartbeat_timeout_seconds before failing) — that also fixes submitting a job seconds before a node reconnects. Deferring resume until after the lifespan yield plus a grace period works too. Note the auditor's option (c) (write the job back to 'queued') is NOT sufficient on its own: nothing in the codebase ever polls for queued jobs, so such a job would sit forever.

title: cancel_job never cancels the task: _active_jobs is keyed by str, the cancel route passes a UUID — the job keeps running and overwrites 'cancelled' with 'completed'
corrected_summary: Job.id is a String(36) column (models.py:477), so submit_job registers _active_jobs[job.id] under a *str* key, while POST /api/jobs/{job_id}/cancel declares job_id: UUID and hands runner.cancel_job a uuid.UUID. The dict lookup at runner.py:228 therefore always misses in production: task.cancel() is never called, the runner keeps executing every remaining step, and when it finishes it writes status='completed' (or 'failed') straight over the 'cancelled' row. This also falsifies the AI Note at runner.py:221-226, which claims the 'cancelled' status written here cannot be overwritten because _run_job only writes terminal status on the success and on_fail='stop' paths — that reasoning holds only if the task really was cancelled. The auditor's finding 7 assumes the server-side task does get cancelled and only the agent is left running; the reality is worse.
failure_scenario: Reproduced end-to-end: a two-step job is submitted with the string id (as jobs.py:277 does), then cancel_job is called with uuid.UUID(job.id) (as jobs.py:551 does). Immediately after cancel the row reads 'cancelled' — so the UI and the 200 response say the job stopped — but the task runs on: both steps execute (step_runs [(0,'success'),(1,'success')]) and the final status is 'completed'. For a real job that means every remaining run_command/gem5 step is dispatched to nodes after the operator cancelled, and the cancellation record is destroyed. Worse, the row is 'cancelled' (a terminal state) in the interim, so DELETE /api/jobs/{id} is allowed to remove it while the runner is still writing step_runs against that id.
fix: Normalise the key on both sides: key _active_jobs by str(job_id) in submit_job and look it up as str(job_id) in cancel_job (and in the finally at runner.py:497). Note tests/integration/test_runner_resume.py:859-890 currently pins this behaviour as 'ACTUAL behaviour ... Reported as POSSIBLE BUG', so that test must be flipped in the same change. Also make _run_job's terminal write conditional on the job not already being 'cancelled', so a lost cancel can never be silently upgraded to 'completed'.

title: DELETE /api/jobs/{id} 500s (IntegrityError) for any job that ever ran a step
refutation_attempt: Tried to refute four ways. (1) Looked for a cascade upstream: models.py:497 `step_runs` and :498 `artifacts` declare only `back_populates`/`order_by` — no `cascade=`, no `passive_deletes`. (2) Checked whether `step_runs.job_id` is really NOT NULL: models.py:537 is `Mapped[str]` (non-Optional), which SQLAlchemy 2.0 renders as NOT NULL, and SQLite enforces NOT NULL independently of PRAGMA foreign_keys — so the author's own AI Note (jobs.py:592-595) claiming SQLite 'succeeds silently' is the part that is wrong. (3) Checked whether SQLAlchemy would skip the nullify for an unloaded collection — it does not; the dependency processor loads and blanks it. (4) Checked for a pinning test: tests/integration/test_jobs_routes.py:537 test_delete_terminal_job uses the `_create_job` helper with zero step runs, so the failing path is untested. Reproduced live: with a completed job + one StepRun, `DELETE /api/jobs/{id}` raises `IntegrityError: (sqlite3.IntegrityError) NOT NULL constraint failed: step_runs.job_id [SQL: UPDATE step_runs SET job_id=? ...] [parameters: (None, '309152fb-...')]`, i.e. a bare 500 in production and the job row survives.
corrected_summary: `await db.delete(job)` relies on SQLAlchemy's default relationship behaviour, which emits `UPDATE step_runs SET job_id=NULL` (and the same for `artifacts`) instead of deleting the children. Both FK columns are NOT NULL, and SQLite enforces NOT NULL regardless of the foreign_keys pragma, so the commit raises IntegrityError and the route returns an unhandled 500 with the job still present. The auditor is right; the only correction is that `artifacts` fails identically, and the author's AI Note at jobs.py:592-595 actively mis-diagnoses SQLite as the safe case.
failure_scenario: Submit any job that executes at least one step (the runner creates a StepRun row per visit at runner.py:384), let it reach `completed`, then press Delete on the Jobs page. Server emits `UPDATE step_runs SET job_id=NULL` -> `sqlite3.IntegrityError: NOT NULL constraint failed: step_runs.job_id` -> bare 500 'Internal Server Error'; the job is not deleted and the UI shows no reason. Only childless jobs (what the tests build) are deletable.
fix: Declare `cascade="all, delete-orphan"` on `Job.step_runs` and `Job.artifacts` in db/models.py (or add an `ops.delete_job` that deletes children first), catch IntegrityError in the route and return 409, and correct the AI Note at jobs.py:589-595.

title: DELETE /api/nodes/{id} 500s (AssertionError) for any node that belongs to a pool
refutation_attempt: Tried to refute by (1) looking for a cascade on `Node.pool_memberships` (models.py:253) and `Pool.node_memberships` (models.py:282) — neither declares one; (2) checking whether SQLAlchemy would just nullify harmlessly as ops.py:648-652's AI Note claims — it cannot, because `pool_node_memberships.node_id` (models.py:304) is part of the composite PK, and SQLAlchemy's sync.clear() raises AssertionError rather than blanking a PK column; (3) checking for a pinning test — tests/integration/test_nodes_routes.py:298 test_deregister_node_204 uses `sample_node`, which conftest never adds to a pool. Reproduced live: node + pool + membership, then `DELETE /api/nodes/{id}` raises `AssertionError: Dependency rule on column 'nodes.id' tried to blank-out primary key column 'pool_node_memberships.node_id'`. Both the route docstring (nodes.py:529, 'via cascade') and ops.py:648-652 ('become genuine orphans') describe outcomes that do not happen.
corrected_summary: `ops.delete_node` (ops.py:657) does `db.delete(node)` with no cascade; SQLAlchemy's default dependency rule tries to blank `pool_node_memberships.node_id`, which is half of that table's composite PK, so the flush raises AssertionError and the route returns an unhandled 500. Neither the node nor the membership is removed. Worth adding: pools.py lets *any* authenticated user add a node to a pool, so a non-admin can render a node permanently undeletable by admins.
failure_scenario: Admin adds node N to pool P (`POST /api/pools/{P}/nodes`), then clicks Delete on the Nodes page. Flush raises `AssertionError: Dependency rule on column 'nodes.id' tried to blank-out primary key column 'pool_node_memberships.node_id'` -> 500 'Internal Server Error'. Membership and node both survive; deregistering a pooled node is impossible until it is manually removed from every pool.
fix: Add `cascade="all, delete-orphan"` to `Node.pool_memberships` (and `Pool.node_memberships`), or have `ops.delete_node` DELETE the membership rows before deleting the node. Fix the contradictory docstrings at nodes.py:529 and ops.py:648-652.

title: POST /api/jobs 500s for any per-step target_node_id/target_pool_id — model_dump() leaves uuid.UUID objects inside the steps_config JSON column
corrected_summary: `steps_config = [s.model_dump() for s in body.steps]` uses plain `model_dump()`, so `StepConfig.target_node_id`/`target_pool_id` (declared `UUID | None` at schemas.py:257-258) stay as `uuid.UUID` objects inside the list handed to `ops.create_job`. That list is bound to the `jobs.steps_config` JSON column, whose serializer is `json.dumps`, which cannot encode a UUID — so the INSERT raises `StatementError: (builtins.TypeError) Object of type UUID is not JSON serializable` and the request returns a bare 500. Per-step targeting is a first-class documented feature (StepConfig docstring, the `.nexus` DSL's `_STEP_KEYWORDS` at parser.py:184, and runner.py:398-402 which reads `step_cfg.get("target_node_id")`), yet it cannot be submitted through the API at all. Job-level targets are unaffected because `ops.create_job` runs them through `_sid()`. This is adjacent to the already-fixed 'raw UUID bound to String(36)' family but is a distinct, still-live site (UUID nested inside a JSON column) and no test covers it — test_jobs_routes.py never submits a per-step target.
failure_scenario: `POST /api/jobs` with `{"name":"pinned","steps":[{"step":"run_command","params":{"command":"echo hi"},"target_node_id":"<node uuid>"}]}` (the API/CLI equivalent of a `.nexus` step carrying `target_node_id`) -> unhandled `TypeError: Object of type UUID is not JSON serializable` inside the INSERT -> 500 'Internal Server Error', no job row created, no usable error message. Verified live for both `target_node_id` and `target_pool_id`; `StepConfig(...).model_dump()` returns `target_node_id: UUID(...)` and `json.dumps` on it raises TypeError.
fix: Use `s.model_dump(mode="json")` at jobs.py:263 (which renders UUIDs as strings, matching what the runner and `ops.get_node_by_id`/`_sid` expect), or coerce the three target fields to `str` before persisting. Add an integration test that submits a step with `target_node_id` and asserts 201 plus a string value in the stored `steps_config`.

title: Credential routes enforce authentication only — any user can read, overwrite, or delete any credential
refutation_attempt: I looked for the missing guard everywhere it could hide: (a) grepped every use of owner_id/is_shared/allowed_groups across packages/ — the only consumers are ops.create_credential, CredentialManager.store, the _cred_to_info projection and the two schemas; nothing reads them for a decision; (b) checked deps.py for a credential-scoped dependency — there is none, and CredMgr/CurrentUser carry no authorization; (c) checked whether the routes are admin-gated by an alias — they use CurrentUser, not AdminUser; (d) checked tests/integration/test_credentials_routes.py — it has no authorization test at all and no PUT test at all, so nothing pins this as intended; (e) checked whether this is the documented 'single-tenant, intentional' posture like artifacts.py's explicit AI Note — it is the opposite: deps.py:238-239 documents require_admin as 'Used by every destructive or infrastructure-mutating route (node registration/provisioning/deletion, storage backend CRUD, credential management)', and ops.py:1226-1228 says 'no ownership or sharing filter is applied here ... The credentials route is responsible for filtering'. Both documented invariants are unimplemented. I then reproduced the whole chain against the real app: admin creates a private git_pat named 'admin-gh' (owner_id==admin, is_shared=False) -> regular user's GET /api/credentials lists it -> PUT returns 200 and credential_manager.get_by_name(db,'admin-gh') then returns {'token': 'BOB-TOKEN', 'username': 'bob'} -> DELETE returns 204. Also confirmed runner.py:708 resolves credential_name via get_by_name with no submitter check.
corrected_summary: Every /api/credentials route uses CurrentUser (authentication only) and no route consults owner_id/is_shared/allowed_groups, so any role=user account can enumerate, re-key (destroying the only copy of the plaintext) or delete another user's private secret. This is not the documented posture: deps.py:238-239 lists 'credential management' among the routes require_admin guards, and ops.list_credentials' docstring (ops.py:1226-1228) explicitly delegates ownership filtering to this route, which never does it.
failure_scenario: Reproduced against the real app: admin POSTs {'name':'admin-gh','credential_type':'git_pat','fields':{'token':'ADMIN-SECRET','username':'admin'},'is_shared':false}. A role=user token then (1) GET /api/credentials -> 200 listing it with owner_id==admin; (2) PUT /api/credentials/{id} with fields={'token':'BOB-TOKEN','username':'bob'} -> 200, and CredentialManager.get_by_name afterwards returns BOB-TOKEN, so every step whose credential_name is 'admin-gh' now authenticates as Bob and the admin's PAT is unrecoverable; (3) DELETE /api/credentials/{id} -> 204, after which every job using it fails with "Credential 'admin-gh' not found". Separately, the same user can submit a job step naming the admin's credential and have the decrypted secret delivered to a node they control.
fix: Add an authorization helper (owner OR admin OR is_shared-and-in-allowed_groups) and apply it in list_credentials (as a filter), update_credential, delete_credential and test_credential; or make the mutating routes AdminUser to match deps.py's documented contract. If unrestricted access really is intended, say so explicitly in the route docstrings the way artifacts.py:89-92 does, and delete the unused owner_id/is_shared/allowed_groups plumbing plus the ops.py note that says the route filters.

title: broadcast_to_dashboards awaits each dashboard send inline on the agent receive loop — one non-reading client stalls step processing cluster-wide
refutation_attempt: I tried three refutations. (1) 'It's only latency, the send will error out': I traced the actual installed stack. uvicorn 0.44.0 + websockets 16.0, no wsproto -> uvicorn/protocols/websockets/auto.py selects WebSocketProtocol (websockets_impl). Its asgi_send does `await self.send(data)` (websockets_impl.py:317) -> websockets/legacy/protocol.py write_frame() -> `await self.drain()` -> _drain_helper(), which parks on a future while the transport is paused (write_limit default 2**16). A peer that never reads therefore blocks the await; it does not raise, so broadcast_to_dashboards' except-clause never fires. (2) 'websockets' keepalive ping will time out and kill the socket, bounding the stall at ~40s': this is the strongest refutation and it FAILS — keepalive_ping (protocol.py:1213) does `pong_waiter = await self.ping()`, and ping() (protocol.py:788) itself ends in `await self.write_frame(True, OP_PING, data)` -> drain(). So the keepalive task blocks on the same flow-control future and never reaches its `asyncio_timeout(self.ping_timeout)` / fail_connection() branch. There is no rescue path. (3) 'The broadcast isn't on the agent's loop': it is — _handle_agent_message awaits it at ws.py:443/467/485/497/502, and that coroutine is awaited inside agent_websocket's `while True: raw = await ws.receive_text()` loop (ws.py:324-335). Also checked that no test pins a slow-client policy (test_ws_routes.py has fan-out and failing-client tests, none with a blocking send) and that the runner has no retry (runner.py: 'no queueing/retry').
corrected_summary: Every agent step message handler awaits broadcast_to_dashboards, which sequentially awaits ws.send_json on each dashboard socket with no timeout and no per-client queue. With the installed uvicorn/websockets stack the send blocks indefinitely on write flow control for a client that stops reading, and the websockets keepalive-ping timeout cannot rescue it (keepalive_ping blocks inside ping() -> write_frame -> drain on the same paused transport), so the agent's receive loop is stalled for as long as the wedged client keeps its TCP connection open. The AI Note at ws.py:191-194 describes this as added 'latency', which understates it.
failure_scenario: A peer opens /ws/dashboard (no auth needed) and never reads. Once ~64KB of frames are buffered, the next step.log from any agent blocks inside `await ws.send_json` at ws.py:199. That agent's `while True: await ws.receive_text()` loop never iterates again, so its subsequent step.completed frame is never read, runner.on_step_completed is never called, and the runner's `asyncio.wait_for(event.wait(), timeout=7200)` burns the full 2h before failing the step with 'Step execution timed out (2h)' — with no retry (runner.py has an explicit 'no queueing/retry' note). Every other agent that emits a step.* frame hits the same blocked socket and wedges the same way.
fix: Bound each send (asyncio.wait_for(ws.send_json(...), timeout≈1s), treating a timeout as a stale client and dropping it) or give each dashboard client a bounded asyncio.Queue drained by its own task, dropping frames when full. Authenticating /ws/dashboard reduces exposure but does not fix the head-of-line blocking (a suspended laptop with an authenticated tab does it too).

title: Frontend addNodeToPool sends {"node_id": ...} but POST /api/pools/{id}/nodes requires a bare JSON array — every "Add Node" click 422s and is silently swallowed
corrected_summary: pools.py:232 declares `node_ids: list[UUID]` as the request body, so FastAPI's generated schema is `{'type':'array','items':{'type':'string','format':'uuid'}}` and the body must be a bare JSON array. client.ts:297 sends `JSON.stringify({ node_id: nodeId })`, an object, which fails validation with 422 'Input should be a valid list'. Pools.tsx:289-299 catches the rejection and only console.errors it, so the row's spinner clears and nothing changes — adding a node to a pool is impossible from the dashboard. Pools.test.tsx:81 mocks api.addNodeToPool wholesale, so no test ever exercises the wire shape, and no backend test covers this body form either.
failure_scenario: Reproduced against the real app: POST /api/pools/{pool_id}/nodes with content '{"node_id": "<uuid>"}' -> 422 {'detail':[{'type':'list_type','loc':['body'],'msg':'Input should be a valid list','input':{'node_id':'...'}}]}; the same call with json=["<uuid>"] -> 201 {'added':[...]}. In the UI an operator opens a pool's slide-over, clicks Add Node, clicks a host row: the spinner appears, api.addNodeToPool 422s, handleAdd's catch logs to the console, onAdded() is never called and the node never joins the pool. Since pool membership is what gates target_pool_id scheduling (pools.py:8-13), pools created through the dashboard can never acquire members.

Add one integration test that posts the exact body the client sends, and stop mocking api.addNodeToPool in the Pools.tsx add-flow test (or assert the serialized body).

title: CPython's subprocess._cleanup() reaps the abandoned child, so a successful run_command/run_script/run_python/gem5 step is reported FAILED with exit_code -1

The author's AI Note at run_command.py:192-200 assumes the only way to reach that branch is a double check() call ('the executor's poll loop returns as soon as it sees a terminal result, so it never calls twice in practice'); it misses this in-process reaper entirely.

After the child exits, one further Popen in the same process — i.e. any concurrently running step on that node (run_script/run_python/git_*/package_install/gem5/docker all call subprocess.run, and asyncio.create_subprocess_shell builds a subprocess.Popen internally), or detect_capabilities() on a reconnect (capability.py:184/238/259) — empties _active and check() then returns StepResult.FAILED with exit_code -1 for a command that exited 0. title: get_latest_step_run orders by random UUID id -> loop iterations get their state/status written onto the wrong step_run row
refutation_attempt: Checked whether the caller makes it moot: ws.py:432 is the only production caller and it is the sole mechanism for locating the row for an incoming step.started frame (there is no step_run_id on the wire — StepStarted carries job_id/step_index/state), so a wrong pick is written blind at ws.py:438-442. corrected_summary: get_latest_step_run orders by StepRun.id DESC, a lexicographic sort over random uuid4 strings, so for a step_index with several attempts it returns an arbitrary attempt. ws.py:432-442 then writes status="running", node_id, the opaque resume `state` and started_at onto whichever row it got — corrupting a finished earlier attempt and leaving the in-flight one with state=NULL (so crash recovery for that attempt has no resume handle).
failure_scenario: A job uses a jump step targeting an earlier index, so index 3 has attempt A (already status="success", finished_at set) and then attempt B. The agent sends step.started for B; get_latest_step_run picks A with ~50% probability; ws.py:438 flips A back to status="running" with a fresh started_at and possibly a different node_id, while B stays status="pending", node_id=NULL, state=NULL. Update the matching notes at ops.py:1114-1119 and models.py:528-531, and flip the xfail at tests/integration/test_db_ops.py:678 once fixed.

title: Agent disconnect mid-step never wakes the runner — job parks for the full 2h
refutation_attempt: I looked for any second wake-up path. (1) Read agent_websocket's finally (ws.py:346-360) in full: disconnect_agent, update_node(status='offline'), broadcast_to_dashboards — no runner callback, and ws.app.state.runner IS in scope there (used at ws.py:452/476). (2) The only setters of a step Event are on_step_completed (runner.py:274-276) and on_step_failed (runner.py:307-309), both driven purely by inbound agent frames. (3) Grepped for a heartbeat-timeout sweeper task that might notice a dead node and act — config.heartbeat_timeout_seconds exists (config.py:122) but nothing in packages/server ever reads it to expire a node or a step. So the wait really is unbounded until 7200s. However I also found a strong reason the auditor's proposed fix is wrong: connection.py:274-281 documents that step tasks are deliberately NOT cancelled on reconnect and deliver their result over the next socket via a ~90s critical-send retry (connection.py:188-211). Since _step_events lives in the same process across the agent's reconnect, waiting is the CORRECT behaviour for a transient blip; failing in-flight steps on every teardown would break that design.
corrected_summary: The server detects node death only via socket teardown, and that teardown does not notify the runner, so a step in flight on a node that truly dies waits the full 7200s ceiling and then fails with the misleading 'Step execution timed out (2h)'. The StepRun stays 'running', the Job stays 'running', and the job's dedicated AsyncSession stays pinned for two hours. Correction to the auditor: failing in-flight steps on disconnect would regress the documented 'a running step survives a reconnect' behaviour — the fix has to be grace-period based, not teardown based.
failure_scenario: Node N is power-cycled 5 s into a 30 s run_command. The socket closes, ws.py marks N offline and the dashboard shows it down; the agent process is gone so no step.failed is ever sent. The runner's coroutine stays parked at runner.py:745 until 7200 s elapse; for those two hours GET /api/jobs/{id} reports the job running on a node the same API reports offline, and the operator's only recourse is cancel (which today does not even stop the task — see the missed finding).
fix: Add a grace-period reaper rather than an on-teardown kill: when a node has been disconnected for longer than heartbeat_timeout_seconds (or after a bounded wait for reconnect), fail the steps whose live dispatch targeted that node via runner.on_step_failed(job_id, idx, f"node {host} went away mid-step"). That requires the runner to track key -> node_id, which _execute_remote_step already has in hand.

title: An unknown on_fail value silently means "continue"
refutation_attempt: I hunted for the missing validation at every layer. schemas.py:256 is a bare `on_fail: str = "stop"` with no Literal and no field validator; StepConfig has no model_config or model_validator; submit_job (jobs.py:212-282) validates only the step name and the params against PARAMS_SCHEMA and never looks at on_fail; parser._parse_trailing_keywords accepts any key="value"; there is no DB constraint (String column via JSON blob). title: The server never sends cancel_step, so cancel and timeout orphan node-side work
refutation_attempt: grep -rn 'cancel_step|CancelStep' over packages/server/src, packages/common/src and packages/agent/src returns only the protocol model (agent_protocol.py:284/296, 416), two docstrings (ws.py:260, base.py:754), and the agent's receive side (connection.py:408-410 -> executor.cancel at executor.py:284). Worth reading together with the missed finding below: because cancel_job's _active_jobs lookup also misses, an API cancel today stops neither the node-side work nor the server-side task.
failure_scenario: An operator cancels a job whose current step is a 6-hour gem5 simulation. The API returns 200 and the row flips to 'cancelled', but no cancel_step frame is sent: gem5 keeps consuming the node's CPU and disk for the remaining hours with its container and m5out directory live, and because _node_matches_step has no exclusivity gate the scheduler happily places the next job's steps on that same node to contend with it. A step that hits the 2h ceiling is abandoned the same way, permanently.

title: submit_job seeds validation context with each step's *params*, so jobs missing required fields are accepted then fail at runtime
refutation_attempt: Tried hard to refute this as intended behaviour. The mechanism IS documented (jobs.py:255-258 calls the ordering deliberate; StepContext's docstring at base.py:67 says outputs 'come from upstream OUTPUT_KEYS and explicit params'; test_jobs_routes.py:223's docstring says 'validated against upstream OUTPUT_KEYS + params'). But no test pins the permissive consequence, and I checked whether the params seeding is load-bearing for the real gem5 chain it was presumably added for — it is not: gem5_run_simulation already declares `m5out_path` in OUTPUT_KEYS (run_simulation.py:155), so OUTPUT_KEYS seeding alone suffices. I then confirmed the runtime side really diverges: runner.py:421-422 merges only `result["outputs"]` (declared OUTPUT_KEYS) into `context.outputs`, and runner.py:359 seeds from `job.context_data`, so a param name never enters the runtime context. Verified end to end: two run_command steps with the 2nd missing `command` -> 201, while that step submitted alone -> 400 'command: required'; and at execution `RunCommandParams(**ctx.resolve(params))` (run_command.py:136) raises pydantic.ValidationError.
corrected_summary: `val_ctx.outputs.update(step_cfg.params)` injects every step's configured parameter *names* into the submit-time context, and RequiredRule (base.py:186-196) treats a name present in `context.outputs` as satisfied. The runner never puts params into the runtime context, so submit-time validation is strictly more permissive than execution and the API's documented 400 contract silently misses real omissions. Reachability caveat the auditor omitted: the field must be entirely absent from params (an empty string still counts as present) and a same-named param must appear on an earlier step, so the JobBuilder UI (which posts every schema field) rarely triggers it — API/CLI/.nexus clients do.
failure_scenario: `POST /api/jobs` with `[{git_clone,{repo_url:...}}, {git_clone,{dest_dir:"/tmp/second"}}]` returns 201 because step 0's `repo_url` param leaked into the validation context. At execution, step 1 resolves against `context.outputs` = {clone_path, commit_sha} and `GitCloneParams(**resolved)` raises a missing-`repo_url` ValidationError on the node — a late runtime failure on a job the API certified valid. Same shape verified for run_command (201 chained vs 400 standalone).
fix: Drop line 259 and seed `val_ctx.outputs` only from `step_cls.OUTPUT_KEYS`; if concrete param values are needed for pass-3 type checking, keep them in a separate dict that RequiredRule/ContextSatisfiableRule do not consult.

title: POST /api/auth/register accepts any role string, commits the row, then 500s on response validation
refutation_attempt: Tried to find validation upstream: `RegisterRequest.role` is a bare `str` (auth.py:76) with no validator; `ops.create_user` (ops.py:146-184) takes `role: str` and commits before returning; `users.role` is `String(16)` with no CHECK constraint (models.py:135); and `UserInfo.role` is typed `UserRole` (schemas.py:126) whose enum admits only admin/manager/user (enums.py:59-61). Ran it: `{"username":"weirdo","password":"pw","role":"superuser"}` -> 500, and `select username, role from users` afterwards returns `('weirdo','superuser')` — the row is committed. Also checked whether login would fail too (which would make the account harmless): it would not — `TokenResponse` (schemas.py:104-106) carries only tokens, no UserInfo, so the broken account can log in and then 500 on `GET /api/auth/me`. No test covers an invalid role.
corrected_summary: `RegisterRequest.role` is an unvalidated `str` while `UserInfo.role` is a `UserRole` enum, so an out-of-enum role is persisted and committed by `ops.create_user` and only then fails Pydantic construction at auth.py:173 — the caller gets a 500 while a permanently unserialisable user row exists. The docstring at auth.py:67-70 documents validation as happening *after* the irreversible write.
failure_scenario: Admin POSTs `{"username":"weirdo","password":"pw","role":"superuser"}` (or a typo like 'Admin'). Row is inserted and committed, then `UserInfo(...)` raises `ValidationError: role Input should be 'admin','manager' or 'user'` -> unhandled 500. The admin believes creation failed, but the account exists and can log in; `GET /api/auth/me` then 500s for that user forever so the dashboard cannot boot for them, and `require_admin`'s string compare denies them everything.
fix: Type the field as `role: UserRole = UserRole.USER` on RegisterRequest so FastAPI rejects it with 422 before any DB write.

title: /ws/dashboard is unauthenticated and streams every job's live stdout plus the whole node inventory
refutation_attempt: I checked whether the guard exists upstream: dashboard_websocket's signature (ws.py:515) takes only `ws`, there is no Depends/token parameter, ws.router is mounted with no dependencies (main.py:272), and deps.py:36-39 states the WS endpoints deliberately use nothing from that module. I checked whether the leak is trivial: StepLog (agent_protocol.py:141-161) carries `stream` and a verbatim `line` of subprocess stdout/stderr, and ws.py:497 forwards the RAW inbound dict, so this really is live stdout of every step. I then weighed it against the 'intended dev defaults' carve-out: this is not admin/admin or 0.0.0.0 — it is an unauthenticated route that should require auth, which the prompt explicitly allows reporting. Two tests (test_ws_routes.py:1745 test_dashboard_ws_connects_without_authentication and :1760 test_dashboard_ws_with_a_bogus_token_is_still_accepted) pin the gap as characterization, and the docstring calls it a 'security gap, knowingly present'. Auditor's cited test line 1743 is the section comment; the def is at 1745.
corrected_summary: dashboard_websocket accepts any socket without reading the ?token= the frontend already appends (useWebSocket.ts:76), and every frame from broadcast_to_dashboards — node.status with hostnames, job.status, and verbatim step.log/step.progress frames carrying raw stdout/stderr lines — is fanned out to it. Real, but knowingly present: the docstring names it and two tests pin it, and on a LAN whose other doors are deliberately open (admin/admin, 0.0.0.0) the marginal escalation is confidentiality of live job output rather than control-plane access — hence medium, not high.
failure_scenario: `websocat ws://nexus:8000/ws/dashboard` with no credentials (or with a revoked/garbage token, per test_dashboard_ws_with_a_bogus_token_is_still_accepted) receives in real time: every node's hostname and online/offline transitions, every job id + step index, and the verbatim stdout/stderr of every running step — which routinely includes tokens echoed by build scripts, `git clone https://user:token@...` URLs and env dumps.
fix: Read the `token` query parameter, validate it with AuthService before manager.connect_dashboard, and close with 4001/4003 on failure. The frontend already sends it, so no client change is needed; the two characterization tests then flip to asserting rejection.

title: Late agent-session teardown evicts the reconnected socket, and no heartbeat ever restores the registry
refutation_attempt: The auditor's central claim is that the test docstring's 'it only recovers on the next heartbeat' is false. I tested exactly that against the real handler: with the node absent from agent_connections, calling _handle_agent_message(..., 'heartbeat', ...) leaves DB status='online' while `str(node.id) in manager.agent_connections` is False. Confirmed. I then searched for any other writer of agent_connections that could repair it — the only one is ConnectionManager.connect_agent, called once per session at ws.py:311; nothing in the heartbeat/register branches re-registers, and there is no reaper. I checked whether the agent would notice and reconnect: it would not — the server keeps answering its heartbeats with `heartbeat_ok` acks on the still-live session-B socket, so connection.py's reconnect loop never triggers. I verified the consequence chain: scheduler.py:141 `if node.status not in ('online','busy')` reads only the DB column, and runner.py returns {'status':'failed','error': f'Agent for node {node.hostname} not connected'} on `sent is False`, with an explicit 'no queueing/retry' note. Downgraded from high because the window is specific (the old server-side socket must outlive the new session's registration — e.g. a network blackhole where the agent's client-side detection beats the server's) and the AI Note at ws.py:346-352 already prescribes the exact fix.
corrected_summary: agent_websocket's `finally` calls manager.disconnect_agent(node_id) unconditionally, so a late-unwinding session evicts a *newer* session's socket and writes status='offline'. The in-code note and the pinning test both claim the node 'recovers on the next heartbeat' — it does not: the heartbeat branch (ws.py:398-404) only writes DB status/last_heartbeat and never calls connect_agent, so the DB flaps back to 'online' with an empty registry entry and the wedge persists for the whole life of the still-healthy connection.
failure_scenario: Verified mechanically: with node X absent from agent_connections, a heartbeat leaves the DB row 'online' and the registry still empty. In production that state is reached when session A's receive_text raises after session B has already registered (network blackhole, then agent-side reconnect). From then on scheduler._node_matches_step accepts X (it reads only node.status), manager.send_to_agent returns False, and every step targeting X fails instantly with 'Agent for node <host> not connected' — permanently, because the server keeps acking the agent's heartbeats so neither side has any reason to reconnect, and there is no step retry.
fix: In the `finally`, only evict/mark offline when `manager.agent_connections.get(node_id) is ws`; have connect_agent close the socket it displaces; and (belt and braces) re-assert registration in the heartbeat branch. Then flip test_agent_ws_teardown_evicts_a_socket_that_already_reconnected's expectations and correct its docstring, which currently asserts a recovery path that does not exist.

title: Node status=online is written outside the try/finally and nothing reaps stale rows, so after a hard restart resume_active_jobs dispatches to nodes with no socket
refutation_attempt: I looked for the reaper the auditor says is missing: grepped every writer of node status/last_heartbeat across packages/server — only ws.py:308 (online, on connect), ws.py:403 (online, on heartbeat) and ws.py:356 (offline, in the finally). main.lifespan (main.py:70-206) has no startup reset and no background sweep, and calls resume_active_jobs at L194, above the `yield` — so ASGI lifespan startup completes before uvicorn accepts any WebSocket upgrade, making agent_connections necessarily empty at that point. resume.py:61-64 calls `await runner.submit_job(...)` per job, which asyncio.create_task()s _run_job immediately, so the tasks run during the loop, long before an agent's 1-60s backoff reconnect. runner.py then returns 'Agent for node <host> not connected' with no retry. However, I have to correct the auditor's causal framing: the position of the online write relative to `try:` is NOT what causes the dominant failure — a kill -9 skips the `finally` no matter where the write sits, and models.py:226-230 already documents 'If the server process dies while agents are connected, rows stay "online" across the restart'. The write's position only matters for the secondary trigger, which is real: connect_agent (and its ws.accept()) is called at L311, outside the try at L323, so an exception there leaves 'online' with no socket and no finally.
corrected_summary: Nothing resets or expires node.status: the WS teardown is its only 'offline' writer, main.lifespan has no startup reset and no heartbeat-expiry sweep, and resume_active_jobs runs before any socket can be accepted. A hard death therefore leaves every row 'online' with zero live sockets, and crash recovery converts running jobs into instantly-failed jobs. The auditor's stated root cause (the online write sitting outside the try/finally) is only the secondary trigger — the stale-after-kill-9 case is independent of that placement and is already documented at models.py:226-230; the resume_active_jobs consequence is the new part.
failure_scenario: Server is kill -9'd with three jobs running. On restart, lifespan runs init_db, builds the runner, then calls resume_active_jobs (main.py:194) — all before uvicorn accepts a WebSocket upgrade, so manager.agent_connections is empty while every node row still reads 'online' from before the crash. Each resumed job task immediately picks a stale-online node (scheduler._node_matches_step reads only node.status), send_to_agent returns False, and the step fails with 'Agent for node X not connected'. There is no retry, so the job is marked failed within milliseconds of startup while the agents are still 1-60s into their reconnect backoff. Secondary: if ws.accept() inside connect_agent (ws.py:311, outside the try at L323) raises, the node is left 'online' with no socket and the finally never runs.
fix: Mark all nodes offline during lifespan startup before resume_active_jobs, and/or add a periodic sweep flipping nodes whose last_heartbeat is older than ~3 heartbeat intervals to offline; have the runner treat 'no live socket' as 'defer/requeue' rather than an immediate terminal failure. Moving the online write inside the try (after connect_agent succeeds) fixes only the accept()-raises case.

title: StorageManager registry is keyed by str id but the routes look it up with a UUID -> backend health is always "Backend not initialized" and POST /transfer always 404s
refutation_attempt: I verified the key types rather than trusting the claim: models.py:417 `id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(36), primary_key=True, default=_new_uuid)`, and manager.py:113 `self._backends[backend_model.id] = instance` — so production keys are `str`. The routes declare `backend_id: UUID` (storage.py:254) and TransferRequest.dest_backend_id is UUID (schemas.py:581), and manager.get_backend does a plain `in` test, so the lookup always misses. I then reproduced production keying exactly (registering the fake under `be.id`, the str, not the test helpers' UUID key): GET /api/storage/backends/{id}/health -> 200 {'healthy': False, 'error': 'Backend not initialized'} for a healthy instance, and POST /api/storage/transfer -> 404 "'Backend <dest> not initialized'" with both backends registered as init_backends would register them. I confirmed the transfer asymmetry: the source lookup uses artifact.storage_backend_id (a str from the ORM) and hits, only the dest lookup (a UUID from the body) misses. Author-flagged in manager.get_backend's own docstring (manager.py:178-181) and pinned by test_storage_routes.py:529 plus frontend/src/pages/Storage.test.tsx. Downgraded from high because the user-visible impact is a wrong red status dot; the transfer path is unreachable anyway since nothing in production ever creates an Artifact row (see the artifacts finding), so no data is lost or mishandled.
corrected_summary: StorageManager.init_backends stores instances under backend_model.id (a str; the column is String(36)) while check_backend_health (storage.py:284) and transfer_artifact's destination lookup pass the FastAPI-converted uuid.UUID, so get_backend always raises KeyError in production. Every healthy backend reports 'Backend not initialized' and POST /api/storage/transfer can never succeed. Author-flagged in the get_backend docstring and already pinned by a characterization test on both the backend and the frontend.
failure_scenario: Reproduced with production keying: a MinIO backend registered and initialized at startup (registry key = str(id)); GET /api/storage/backends/{id}/health returns 200 {'healthy': false, 'error': 'Backend not initialized'} — a red dot for a perfectly healthy backend, and a message whose own AI Note misdiagnoses it as 'registered after server startup'. POST /api/storage/transfer with both backends str-keyed returns 404 "'Backend <dest-uuid> not initialized'" after flipping the transfer row to 'failed'.
fix: Normalize on one representation — coerce in StorageManager.get_backend and init_backends (str(backend_id)) — then flip test_health_check_str_keyed_instance_reports_not_initialized to expect healthy=True, collapse _register_fake_both into _register_fake, and update the Storage.test.tsx note.

title: StorageManager registry keyed by str id but every route looks it up by UUID -> backend health always reports "Backend not initialized"
refutation_attempt: I checked whether the two representations could ever compare equal: models.py:76-86 `_new_uuid()` returns `str(uuid.uuid4())` and the column is `String(36)`, so `backend_model.id` is a plain `str`; the path parameter in routes/storage.py:253-254 is annotated `backend_id: UUID`, so FastAPI hands the handler a `uuid.UUID`. `uuid.UUID.__hash__` is `hash(self.int)`, so a UUID key can never hit a str-keyed dict entry. I checked for a normalization layer inside get_backend (manager.py:191-193): it is a raw `in` test with no `_sid()`/`str()` coercion, and its own docstring (manager.py:178-181) concedes 'lookups must use the same representation, not a converted UUID'. I checked whether a test contradicts the claim: tests/integration/test_storage_routes.py:529-563 is a passing characterization test asserting healthy=False for a str-keyed healthy instance, and the helpers `_register_fake` (:183-199) and `_register_fake_both` (:576-596) exist purely to work around it. All 146 tests pass. Not refuted — but the severity is inflated.
corrected_summary: init_backends stores instances under the str `backend_model.id` while get_backend is always called with the route's `uuid.UUID`, so every genuinely initialized backend misses the registry. Verified. Severity is medium, not high: the only *reachable* consequence is that `GET /api/storage/backends/{id}/health` permanently reports healthy=false/"Backend not initialized", plus `POST /api/storage/transfer` 404ing on its destination lookup. `upload_artifact(backend_id=UUID)` is unreachable — it has zero non-test callers (I confirmed `create_artifact` in db/ops.py:1395 is called only from manager.py:262, and nothing calls upload_artifact), so no data path is broken today. Note the asymmetry: the *source* lookup in transfer_artifact (manager.py:357) uses `artifact.storage_backend_id`, a str, and therefore hits, which is why the destination is always the one that fails.
failure_scenario: Operator configures a working MinIO backend; startup logs "Initialized storage backend: primary" and the instance lands under key `'a1b2...'` (str). The dashboard Storage page calls `GET /api/storage/backends/a1b2.../health` -> routes/storage.py:284 `mgr.get_backend(UUID('a1b2...'))` -> manager.py:191 `UUID not in {str: ...}` -> KeyError -> route returns `{"healthy": false, "error": "Backend not initialized"}`. The operator cannot distinguish this from a real outage. Same miss makes every `POST /api/storage/transfer` return 404 on the destination.
fix: Normalize inside the manager: `self._backends[str(backend_model.id)] = instance` in init_backends and `backend_id = str(backend_id)` at the top of get_backend (the `_sid()` pattern db/ops.py:73 already uses). Then flip the expectations in test_health_check_str_keyed_instance_reports_not_initialized and collapse the two test helpers.

title: local_ipv4s(): the `ip -4 addr` fallback can never run when ifconfig is absent
refutation_attempt: I re-read provisioner.py:288-296 line by line: both `subprocess.run(["ifconfig"], ...)` (289) and the `if not out:` fallback to `["ip", "-4", "addr"]` (291) sit inside ONE try whose handler is `except Exception: pass` (295-296). subprocess.run raises FileNotFoundError when the binary is absent, so control leaves the try before line 291 is ever evaluated. I checked whether the docstring intends this: no — lines 264-270 promise 'Two discovery passes, each individually wrapped in try/except' and '``ifconfig`` (falling back to ``ip -4 addr``)'. I checked the tests: tests/unit/test_provisioner.py:508-522 justifies the fallback with 'Minimal container images ship ``ip`` but not ``ifconfig``' and asserts `sub.calls == [['ifconfig'], ['ip','-4','addr']]` — but only for the ifconfig-exits-0-with-empty-output case; the missing-binary test at :554-559 asserts `local_ipv4s() == ['192.168.1.50']`, i.e. the UDP address only, with `ip` never invoked. So the code cannot serve its own documented motivating case. Not refuted.
corrected_summary: The `ip -4 addr` fallback is nested in the same try block as the `ifconfig` invocation and only runs when ifconfig executes and prints nothing. A missing ifconfig binary raises FileNotFoundError straight into `except Exception: pass`, skipping the fallback — which matters more than the auditor implied, because net-tools is not installed by default on modern Ubuntu/Debian/RHEL, so the entire second discovery pass is effectively dead on a typical Linux server host and only the single UDP-probe address is ever returned.
failure_scenario: Nexus server on a minimal Debian/Ubuntu host with no net-tools and two NICs — 10.0.0.5 on the default route, 192.168.50.5 on the lab LAN where the device lives. `subprocess.run(["ifconfig"])` raises FileNotFoundError, the `ip -4 addr` pass is skipped, and local_ipv4s() returns only ['10.0.0.5']. callback_candidates() hands the installer [hostname, 10.0.0.5]; if the mDNS hostname does not resolve on the device, the installer's WS handshake probe fails on every candidate and provisioning aborts with exit 7 / NO_WS_ROUTE, forcing the operator to hand-pin ws_host.
fix: Split into two independent try blocks (as the UDP probe already is), or wrap only the ifconfig call in `except (FileNotFoundError, OSError)` and fall through to `ip -4 addr`. Then extend the missing-binary test to assert `sub.calls == [['ifconfig'], ['ip','-4','addr']]`.

title: Node API key passed in remote argv twice -> readable via `ps` by any local user on the provisioned device
refutation_attempt: I looked for an existing equivalent exposure that would make this redundant: the agent's persisted config IS protected — packages/agent/src/nexus_agent/config.py:107-114 writes the JSON then `os.chmod(path, 0o600)`, and its own docstring (line 18) says so. So the argv exposure is a genuinely distinct, longer-lived (multi-minute install) leak, not a duplicate of an already-world-readable file. I confirmed the two argv sites: provisioner.py:526-530 builds `bash /tmp/nexus-install.sh ... {_q(api_key)} ...` and runs it through `client.exec_command` (line 478), which makes the SSH server exec `$SHELL -c '<cmd>'` so the whole string lands in the remote process table; INSTALL_SH line 159 re-exposes it as `"$AGENT" init --server "$WS" --api-key "$KEY"`. I confirmed the escalation is real rather than theoretical: routes/ws.py connect_agent carries an explicit AI Note that 'a duplicate agent process would hijack step delivery for that node' (self.agent_connections[node_id] = ws silently replaces the entry). Two limits I could NOT refute away but that cap severity: on macOS a non-root user cannot read another user's argv (KERN_PROCARGS2 is uid-restricted), so the leak is Linux-specific; and the module docstring's 'Passwords are held in memory only and never logged' (line 9) is about the SSH password, which is indeed never on a command line.
corrected_summary: The node api_key is passed as a positional argv element to /tmp/nexus-install.sh (provisioner.py:528) and again as `--api-key "$KEY"` to `nexus-agent init` (INSTALL_SH line 159), so on a Linux target it is world-readable via /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the whole multi-minute install. This is a real escalation beyond the documented trust model because the persisted config is chmod 0600 — the argv window is the only way a *different* local account learns the key — and with it that account can open /ws/agent/<node_id> and silently displace the real agent (ws.py connect_agent AI Note), receiving step dispatches meant for it. On macOS targets the leak does not apply (argv of other users' processes is not readable).
failure_scenario: Operator provisions Linux lab machine build07 over SSH as user `ci`. During the install (venv creation + three pip installs + a per-candidate WS probe), unprivileged local account `student` runs `ps auxww | grep nexus-install` (or reads /proc/<pid>/cmdline) and gets the node api_key in cleartext. It then connects to ws://server:8000/ws/agent/<node_id>?api_key=<key>; connect_agent overwrites the registry entry without closing the real agent's socket, so subsequent `execute_step` frames for that node — including any `credential_config` the server inlines — are delivered to `student` instead.
fix: Never put the key on a command line. Write it to a 0600 file over the already-open SFTP channel (or pipe it on the installer's stdin) and have INSTALL_SH read it from there and shred it; have `nexus-agent init` accept the key from an env var or stdin instead of argv.

title: Provisioner writes /tmp/nexus-install.sh to a fixed path with no O_EXCL -> symlink pre-creation gives arbitrary file overwrite as the SSH user
refutation_attempt: I attacked the exact mechanism the auditor claimed. The symlink variant is largely BLOCKED on Linux: systemd ships `fs.protected_symlinks=1` in /usr/lib/sysctl.d/50-default.conf, and that rule refuses to follow a symlink in a world-writable sticky directory when the symlink's owner matches neither the follower nor the directory owner — so root (or `ci`) following mallory's /tmp symlink gets EACCES. So the auditor's stated primitive does not work on a default systemd Linux box. It DOES work on macOS, which has no equivalent protection and is a first-class provisioning target here (INSTALL_SH lines 185-202 install a launchd job, and provision() brew-installs python@3.12). More importantly, while trying to refute it I found a stronger variant that defeats protected_symlinks entirely and works on both platforms, so the finding survives with a corrected mechanism. I confirmed the code: provisioner.py:519-521 `sftp = client.open_sftp(); sftp.putfo(io.BytesIO(INSTALL_SH.encode()), "/tmp/nexus-install.sh")` — a compile-time-constant path, paramiko's putfo opens mode 'wb' (O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, no O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW) — and the same literal is the argument to `bash` at line 527, a separate exec_command round trip.
corrected_summary: The remote installer is uploaded to the constant path /tmp/nexus-install.sh with no O_EXCL and then executed in a *separate* SSH round trip. The auditor's symlink primitive is blocked on default systemd Linux (fs.protected_symlinks=1) but works on macOS, which this module explicitly supports. The stronger, platform-independent variant is a pre-created *regular* file: mallory creates /tmp/nexus-install.sh mode 0666 that she owns; putfo truncates and writes into it (she still owns it, so she can rewrite it); between the putfo at line 520 and `bash /tmp/nexus-install.sh ...` at line 527 she overwrites the contents and the provisioning user executes her script — code execution as the SSH user (commonly root), which is strictly worse than the arbitrary-write the auditor described.
failure_scenario: On lab machine build07, unprivileged local user mallory pre-creates /tmp/nexus-install.sh (mode 0666, owned by her) long before any provisioning, and busy-loops rewriting it with her payload. An operator later provisions build07 over SSH as root. `sftp.putfo` truncates and writes INSTALL_SH into mallory's file; mallory's loop immediately rewrites it; the next round trip runs `bash /tmp/nexus-install.sh <py> nexus <repo> <branch> <cands> <port> <api_key> <node_id> <mode>` — executing mallory's code as root and handing her the node api_key in argv. On macOS the simpler `ln -s /etc/cron.d/nexus /tmp/nexus-install.sh` variant also works, since there is no protected_symlinks equivalent.
fix: Upload to an unpredictable per-run path with exclusive semantics: `run("mktemp")` first (or derive a name from `secrets.token_hex(16)` under the SSH user's $HOME rather than /tmp), putfo to that path, execute it, then `rm -f` it. Combined with moving the api_key off argv, this closes both provisioner findings at once.

title: execute()'s except handlers can raise → zero terminal messages → job hangs for the full 7200s runner timeout
refutation_attempt: I reproduced both triggers against the real StepExecutor with a fake connection: (A) startup() returning None → StepStarted validation error at 191 → except at 258 → AttributeError inside _capture with 0 messages sent; (B) state["exit_code"]="not-an-int" + a raising check() → ValidationError inside the handler with only step.started sent. I then tried to refute reachability: I AST-scanned all 13 shipped steps in packages/steps — every startup() returns a dict on every path (docker/ensure_container.py and gem5/collect_results.py end in a try but every branch returns a dict), and every exit_code written is an int literal or a subprocess returncode. So neither trigger fires with shipped steps; it needs a new/third-party step. I also checked the runner: runner.py:745 really does wait 7200s on _step_events[key], so the hang is real once triggered. Finally, the original exception IS logged with exc_info at executor.py:259 before the secondary failure, so there is a local trace (the auditor implies total silence).
corrected_summary: execute()'s docstring promises "Never raises", but the terminal-message emission inside both except handlers is unguarded: _capture() does state.get(...) on whatever startup() returned (AttributeError at executor.py:498, not 518 as claimed) and StepFailed(exit_code=...) validates a state-supplied value. A step whose startup() returns a non-dict, or puts a non-int-coercible exit_code in state, therefore makes execute() raise with no terminal message. None of the 13 shipped steps do either, so this is a hardening gap on a pluggable-step boundary rather than a live bug.
failure_scenario: A newly added FlowStep whose startup() falls off the end (returns None) is dispatched: StepStarted(state=None) raises ValidationError at executor.py:191 → the except at 258 calls _capture at 260 → AttributeError at 498 ('NoneType' object has no attribute 'get') escapes execute(). Because execute() is a detached create_task (connection.py:406) nothing retrieves the exception, the server never receives step.started or a terminal frame, and JobRunner._execute_remote_step blocks on _step_events[key].wait() for 7200s (runner.py:745) before failing the job with a timeout instead of the real error.

title: startup()/check() run inline on the event loop and shipped steps block it for minutes
refutation_attempt: The premise checks out and is broader than reported: I verified blocking subprocess.run inside startup() in six shipped steps, not three — git/clone.py:162 (timeout=600, startup at 97), git/pull.py:143 (300), package/install.py:193 (600), system/update_software.py:241-273 (120+30+600), gem5/collect_results.py:228/276 (600 tar + 600 upload), docker/ensure_container.py:_docker(timeout=validated.timeout, default 600). Two of those three gem5-pipeline steps are core to the flagship workflow. But I refuted two of the auditor's three impacts: (1) nothing in the server, CLI or frontend ever sends cancel_step (repo-wide grep: only the agent listener and tests reference it; runner.cancel_job at runner.py:228-232 explicitly does not send one, per its own AI Note at 214-220), so no cancel is "dropped"; (2) no shipped step reaches _run_subprocess (AST scan: none of the 13 startups emit a "command" key; three explicitly document that they must not), so no co-resident stream_pipe exists to stall. Confirmed the rest: scheduler.py:135 says "busy counts as schedulable" so concurrent steps per node are normal, and server config heartbeat_timeout_seconds (config.py:122) is never consumed, so the node stays "online" with stale telemetry rather than being failed over.
corrected_summary: step.startup() (line 174) and step.check() (lines 453, 566) are called synchronously on the asyncio event loop, and six of the thirteen shipped steps run blocking subprocess.run inside startup() with 120–600s timeouts — including docker_ensure_container and gem5_collect_results, two thirds of the flagship gem5 pipeline. One such step freezes the whole agent process: the listener reads no frames, other steps' poll loops never fire, pending critical sends stall, and no heartbeat goes out. The auditor's cancel-related and pipe-buffer impacts do not apply (no cancel_step is ever sent, and no shipped step uses the streaming subprocess path).
failure_scenario: Node A is running a gem5 poll step for job 1 when job 2's docker_ensure_container lands on it and has to pull a fresh image. startup() blocks the event loop in subprocess.run(..., timeout=600) for up to 10 minutes. During that window: job 1's _poll_step never wakes, so its already-finished simulation is not reported until the pull ends; a step.completed that was mid-retry in send_message stays unsent; no heartbeats are emitted so the Nodes UI shows "last heartbeat 10 minutes ago" with stale load/active_steps while the node still reads online (nothing consumes heartbeat_timeout_seconds); and any execute_step frame the server dispatches to this node sits unread in the socket buffer for the full 10 minutes while the runner silently waits on its 7200s timer.
fix: Offload the sync hooks: `state = await asyncio.to_thread(step.startup, params, ctx)` at line 174 and `result = await asyncio.to_thread(running.step.check, running.state)` at lines 453 and 566. _running_steps mutation stays on the loop thread either way, so the no-lock invariant in the class docstring is preserved.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: The agent silently drops credential_config, so every credentialed step runs with no credential
corrected_summary: execute() never reads cmd.credential_config, and StepContext has no field to carry it (base.py:88-95), so the decrypted credential the server resolves and transmits is discarded on arrival. Worse, the server pops credential_name out of params as a security boundary (runner.py:696-701), so the step cannot recover the reference either — the credential feature is end-to-end non-functional for remote steps. Author-flagged at executor.py:125-128 and again at git/clone.py:22 and git/pull.py:19.
failure_scenario: A user creates a credential named 'gitlab-token' and submits a job whose git_clone step sets credential_name: gitlab-token on a private repo. The server validates the param, resolves and decrypts the credential, pops credential_name from params and sends the plaintext in ExecuteStepCommand.credential_config (runner.py:701-719). The agent builds StepContext at executor.py:159 without it, so git_clone's subprocess.run of `git clone` (clone.py:162) runs unauthenticated and fails with an auth error after up to 600s — with no indication anywhere in the job log that the configured credential was never applied.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: Cancelling a job never stops the work on the node
corrected_summary: cancel_job() cancels only the server-side coroutine and writes status=cancelled; it never sends a CancelStepCommand. A repo-wide grep confirms nothing in packages/server, packages/cli or frontend/src emits a cancel_step frame, so the agent's entire cancel path (executor.cancel, the 5s kill escalation, and every FlowStep.cancel hook) is dead code outside tests. failure_scenario: A user cancels a running gem5 job from the UI. title: DashboardJobCompleted is a defined-but-never-emitted wire frame -> finished jobs display as "Running" forever
refutation_attempt: I tried to find a producer three ways: (a) grepped all of packages/ for DashboardJobCompleted and "job.completed" — only the class def (agent_protocol.py:384), the union (421), and frontend consumers (types/index.ts:366, stores/index.ts:416, stores/index.test.ts:587-591); (b) grepped for broadcast/broadcast_to_dashboards across packages/server — every call site is in ws.py (319, 358, 443, 467, 485, 497, 502) and none in runner/; (c) read runner._run_job in full (runner.py:311-497): the three terminal writes (451-456 failed, 469-472 completed, plus cancel_job at 231) do only ops.update_job with no ws call, and the runner holds self._ws only for send_to_agent. I also checked for a client-side fallback: no setInterval/refetchInterval anywhere in frontend/src except JobDetail.tsx:547/598, so the Jobs list has no poll. Two things narrow the impact and lower severity from the auditor's "high": JobDetail.tsx polls every 3s while a job is active, so the detail page self-heals; and agent_protocol.py:316-320 states as design that dashboard frames are "UI notifications, not state" and that a client which misses one "recovers by re-fetching over REST". So the real damage is a stale row on the Jobs list until remount/filter change, not lost state.
corrected_summary: DashboardJobCompleted (type "job.completed") has zero construction sites in the server: no code path broadcasts a job's terminal status, so the last live frame a job emits is DashboardJobStatus(status="running") from ws.py:467. The Jobs list row therefore stays "Running" until the user remounts the page or changes the filter. ws.py:464-466's comment ("The runner emits the job's terminal status once it advances past the last step") is factually wrong — the terminal writes are runner.py:451-456 (failed), 469-472 (completed) and cancel_job at runner.py:231, none of which broadcast.
failure_scenario: Submit a 2-step job and leave /jobs open. On the last step.completed, ws.py:467 broadcasts job.status with status="running"; runner.py:469 then writes status="completed" and broadcasts nothing. Jobs.tsx only fetches in the useEffect at 163-167 (mount + filter change), so the row keeps its "Running" badge and its duration keeps counting from Date.now() (Jobs.tsx:115) indefinitely.
