Note completed_at is a bare datetime on this model (agent_protocol.py:398), not UTCDateTime, so it must be passed tz-aware or the frontend re-hits the naive-timestamp bug on this path. Also correct the stale assertion in the ws.py:464-466 comment.

title: `${var}` param interpolation is published in the OpenAPI contract but implemented nowhere -> shell silently expands it to empty string
refutation_attempt: I looked for the substitution in every plausible place: StepContext.resolve (base.py:90-108) is a two-line key-level dict merge with no regex/format; runner._execute_local_step (540) and _execute_remote_step (691-692) call only context.resolve + resolve_for_os; the agent does the same resolve_for_os pass and never rewrites strings. grep for '${' across packages/*/src returns only docstrings (schemas.py:239/360, runner.py:515/629, db/models.py:457/520, db/ops.py:1013) plus parser.py's parse-time @set expansion (_substitute_vars, which by design leaves unknown vars intact). I confirmed the claim reaches OpenAPI: '${var}' in StepConfig.model_json_schema()['description'] is True. I checked whether the shell might have the variable in its environment: executor.py:382 uses create_subprocess_shell with no env= argument, and neither run_command.py nor the executor injects context into os.environ, so an unset ${x} expands to "". tests/unit/test_parser.py:110-121 asserts the placeholder "survives for the runner to resolve" — i.e. the test itself documents a resolver that does not exist. I lowered severity to medium because there is no user-facing doc surface other than FastAPI /docs, and the auditor's own example (`cd ${clone_path} && make`) actually fails loudly (cd to $HOME, then make finds no makefile); the silently-wrong outcomes need a forgiving command (e.g. `cp x ${dir}/`).
corrected_summary: The ${var} placeholder substitution promised by StepConfig.params (schemas.py:239, which is published in the OpenAPI schema) and repeated by runner.py:515/629 and db/models.py:457/520 does not exist anywhere in packages/. The only "resolution" is StepContext.resolve's key-name merge, so chaining works only when a downstream param name exactly equals an upstream OUTPUT_KEY; a ${...} string is passed verbatim to the step and, for shell-backed steps, expanded to the empty string by the target shell.
failure_scenario: POST /api/jobs with [{git_clone, repo_url:...}, {run_command, command:"cp build/out ${clone_path}/artifacts/"}]. Submit validation passes (a valid str). The agent receives the literal command, create_subprocess_shell (executor.py:382) expands the unset ${clone_path} to "", and the copy lands at /artifacts/ instead of inside the clone — exit code 0 in the common case, so the step reports success and the job completes wrong.
fix: Either implement the substitution where the docstrings claim it (expand ${k} from context.outputs while walking params inside StepContext.resolve / runner._execute_remote_step), or strike the claim from schemas.py:239, schemas.py:360, runner.py:515/629, db/models.py:457/520, db/ops.py:1013 and parser.py:18-21 and document that chaining is by OUTPUT_KEY name only.

title: Submit-time validation context is seeded with every step's explicit params, which do not exist at runtime -> invalid plan accepted with 200, explodes on the node after prior steps have run
refutation_attempt: I tried to find a compensating guard and to prove the path unreachable. Replayed the exact submit loop (jobs.py:228-259) and the exact runtime path in-process with the real registry: both run_command steps validate clean, val_ctx ends as {'exit_code': None, 'stdout_path': None, 'stderr_path': None, 'command': './long_build.sh'}, while the runtime StepContext.resolve({}) + resolve_for_os yields {'shell': '/bin/bash', 'exit_code': 0, 'stdout_path': ..., 'stderr_path': ...} and RunCommandStep().startup(...) raises pydantic ValidationError "command Field required". So the asymmetry is real and produces a runtime failure, exactly as claimed. I checked whether a test pins the params-merge as intended: test_jobs_routes.py:223-243 (test_submit_multi_step_accumulates_upstream_outputs) supplies an explicit command on BOTH steps, so it pins only the OUTPUT_KEYS threading, not the params leak. I did correct the auditor's anchor: base.py:197 (RequiredRule accepting a context hit) is explicitly documented as intended (base.py:189-196), so the defect line is jobs.py:259, not base.py. Severity reduced to medium: the outcome is a late job FAILED with a confusing error, no corruption, and jobs.py:255-259 shows the merge exists for a real reason (letting a concrete value beat a None placeholder for pass-3 typing).
corrected_summary: jobs.py:259 (`val_ctx.outputs.update(step_cfg.params)`) makes the submit-time validation context a strict superset of the runtime context, which the runner builds from harvested OUTPUT_KEYS only (runner.py:421-422). Because RequiredRule (base.py:197) accepts any key present in context.outputs, a step that is genuinely missing a required param can be satisfied by an unrelated earlier step's param of the same name, so the plan is accepted (201) and only fails when the agent runs it. jobs.py:223-226's claim that this "mirrors, at submission time, the context the runner will build" is inaccurate.
failure_scenario: POST /api/jobs with steps [{"step":"run_command","params":{"command":"./long_build.sh"}},{"step":"run_command","params":{}}] returns 201. Verified in-process: step 1 validates clean because val_ctx.outputs["command"] leaked from step 0; at runtime step 1's context has only exit_code/stdout_path/stderr_path, so startup() raises ValidationError "command Field required" on the node — after step 0 has burned its full runtime (hours for a gem5 step).
fix: Drop the params merge at jobs.py:259 so the validation context is OUTPUT_KEYS-only, and instead special-case the one case it was added for (a key that is both an OUTPUT_KEY of the step and explicitly provided to it) by overwriting only those keys. Also amend base.py:66-67, which describes StepContext.outputs keys as coming from "upstream OUTPUT_KEYS and explicit params" without noting that the params half exists only in the validation lifetime.

title: `StepConfig.on_fail` is an unvalidated `str` and the runner compares `== "stop"` -> any misspelling fails OPEN (job continues past a fatal step and reports COMPLETED)
refutation_attempt: I looked for validation at every layer that could close the hole. StepConfig.on_fail is a bare `str` with no validator and no model_config (verified: StepConfig(step='x', on_fail='CONTINUE').on_fail == 'CONTINUE'); JobSubmit adds nothing; jobs.submit_job validates only step names and params (jobs.py:229-244) and never inspects on_fail; the parser deliberately does not validate it, and tests/unit/test_parser_edge_cases.py:995-1001 pins that non-validation with the rationale "enum validation belongs to the schema layer" / "POST /api/jobs is the validation boundary" — a boundary that does not in fact validate, which strengthens the finding rather than refuting it. runner.py:372 reads step_cfg.get("on_fail", "stop") and runner.py:451 is the only comparison, so anything other than the exact lowercase "stop" takes the continue branch and the job ends COMPLETED at runner.py:469. I checked tests/integration/test_runner_scheduler.py:490-540: it covers only the exact "stop" default and the exact "continue" value, so no test pins the unknown-value behavior. The JobBuilder is not a source of typos (it does not expose on_fail), so the reachable paths are the raw API, a .nexus file, and a saved template.
corrected_summary: on_fail is typed as an unconstrained str (schemas.py:256) and the runner's only test is `if on_fail == "stop"` (runner.py:451), so every value except the exact lowercase "stop" — including "Stop", "STOP", "halt", 5 (the parser lifts non-strings verbatim) — silently selects the continue path. The safe default therefore fails open on a typo, and the job finishes with status COMPLETED at runner.py:469-472 despite a fatal step failure.
failure_scenario: POST /api/jobs (or a .nexus line, or a saved template) with a step carrying on_fail="Stop". StepConfig accepts it verbatim; when that step fails, runner.py:451 takes the else branch, sets context.outputs["_last_failed"] and advances, every later step runs against a broken workspace, and runner.py:469 marks the job "completed" — the Jobs list shows a green job that actually failed.
fix: Type it as on_fail: Literal["stop", "continue"] = "stop" in schemas.py:256 so a bad value is a 422/400 at submit, and invert runner.py:451 to `if on_fail != "continue":` so unknown values fail closed. (target_os at schemas.py:259 has the same loose typing but fails closed via "No available node for step ... (os=...)", so it is not urgent.)

title: `timeout` param on run_command/run_script/run_python is documented as a maximum execution time but is enforced nowhere
refutation_attempt: Searched for any consumer of the stored value: `grep -rn 'state\["timeout"\]|state.get("timeout")' packages/{agent,server,common,steps}/src` returns nothing at all, so no component reads it. Read check() in full for all four steps (run_command.py:179-219, run_script.py:172-210, python/run.py:275-331, run_simulation.py:297-364) — no elapsed-time comparison and no start timestamp is ever recorded. Checked whether a test pins enforcement: tests/unit/test_steps/test_shell_steps.py only asserts the ge=1/le=86400 bounds (:289-302, :525-529) and that state['timeout']==3600 (:73) — nothing asserts an effect. Reproduced live with .venv/bin/python: startup({'command':'sleep 6','timeout':1}) then check() at 1 s/2 s/3 s/4 s returned RUNNING every time with state['timeout']==1. Confirmed the only backstop is runner.py:745 wait_for(timeout=7200) and that no cancel is sent to the agent when it expires (runner.py:753-754 just returns failed), matching the AI Note at executor.py:557-560.
corrected_summary: All three shell/python steps publish `timeout: int = Field(3600, description="Maximum execution time in seconds.", ge=1, le=86400)` to /api/steps and the JobBuilder UI, store it in state, and never compare it against elapsed time; no startup timestamp is recorded, so the value is structurally unusable. gem5_run_simulation has the same dead field but is author-flagged (run_simulation.py:197-199); the other three are not flagged anywhere. Severity is medium rather than high: the step still terminates when its child does, so the damage is a false published contract plus a 2 h pin on the job and an orphaned child afterwards, not incorrect results.
failure_scenario: A user submits run_command with command="curl https://unreachable-host" and timeout=60 expecting failure after a minute. Reproduced: with timeout=1 and `sleep 6`, check() returned RUNNING at t=1,2,3,4 s. _poll_step (executor.py:565-575) has no timeout guard, so the step stays RUNNING until the child exits; the job is pinned to runner.py:745's 7200 s ceiling and then reported 'Step execution timed out (2h)'. No cancel_step is sent on that path, so the agent's poll loop and the child keep running indefinitely and executor.active_count never drops — the node reports itself busy in every heartbeat until the agent process is restarted.
fix: Record `"started_at": time.time()` in startup()'s state, and in check() — after the WNOHANG poll returns (0,0) — compare `time.time() - state["started_at"] > state["timeout"]`; on breach os.killpg the group, set state["error"] and state["exit_code"] = -1 and return FAILED. Same change in run_command.py, run_script.py, python/run.py and gem5/run_simulation.py. Alternatively drop the field from the three schemas so the UI stops advertising it.

title: _unhide_editable_pth() globs the base interpreter's lib dir, not the venv's, so the fix it exists for never runs
refutation_attempt: Tried to show resolve() stays inside the venv. Ran in this repo's venv: sys.executable = <repo>/.venv/bin/python, Path(sys.executable).is_symlink() = True, .resolve() = /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/bin/python3.14, so lib_dir as coded = /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/lib (exists, but glob returns []). The un-resolved form globs the three real shims (_editable_impl_nexus_server/common/steps.pth). So the helper can never touch the files it exists for on any stock `python -m venv` layout — and INSTALL_SH (nexus_deploy.py:216-241) builds nodes with exactly `"$PY" -m venv .venv`. Strongest corroboration: dev.sh:181 performs the identical fix with the CORRECT pattern (`chflags nohidden .venv/lib/python*/site-packages/_editable_impl_nexus_*.pth`), so the author's own working implementation contradicts this one. Tried to find an alternative recovery path: `grep -rn chflags` over the repo shows nexus_deploy.py's INSTALL_SH has no chflags at all, so on a node this dead helper is the only such mechanism. Confirmed zero test coverage: tests/unit/test_steps/test_misc_steps.py references _detect_repo_dir (:2062) but never _unhide_editable_pth, and :2027 only stubs the chflags call as 'succeeding'.
corrected_summary: `Path(venv_python).resolve()` follows the venv's bin/python symlink out to the base interpreter, so `.parent.parent / "lib"` is the system Python's lib dir and the `_editable_impl_*.pth` glob always returns []; no chflags ever runs on the files this helper was written to un-hide. Verified empirically, and contradicted by dev.sh:181 which does the same fix with the correct un-resolved path. Severity is medium rather than high because the triggering condition (setuptools leaving UF_HIDDEN on a freshly written .pth, macOS only) is rare — but when it does occur the helper is 100 % dead and the node bricks itself.
failure_scenario: update_software runs on a macOS node; pip reinstalls the three editable packages and setuptools leaves UF_HIDDEN set on .venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/_editable_impl_nexus_common.pth. _unhide_editable_pth(sys.executable) globs /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/lib/python*/site-packages/_editable_impl_*.pth, matches nothing, and returns silently. The step reports done:True and schedules the restart; site.addpackage skips the hidden .pth, so the restarted agent dies with ModuleNotFoundError: nexus_common. The node is permanently offline, and update_software cannot be re-run to heal it because that is the only self-heal path — and the SSH re-provision path (nexus_deploy.py INSTALL_SH) carries no chflags step either, so it may not recover it.
fix: Do not resolve(): `lib_dir = Path(venv_python).parent.parent / "lib"`, or better ask the interpreter itself — `subprocess.run([venv_python, "-c", "import sysconfig;print(sysconfig.get_paths()['purelib'])"])` — and glob `_editable_impl_*.pth` there. Add a unit test asserting the globbed directory is inside the venv, and consider adding the same chflags line to nexus_deploy.py's INSTALL_SH so the SSH recovery path works too.

title: gem5_run_simulation.check() runs an unguarded subprocess after recording success, so a wedged docker daemon reports a successful simulation as FAILED
refutation_attempt: Tried to find a guard on the propagation path. run_simulation.py:344-354: state['exit_code'] is written at :341, then the probe at :349 runs with timeout=30 and no try/except. executor.py:565-575 `_poll_step` calls `running.step.check(running.state)` bare. executor.py:258-274 catches it and builds StepFailed(error=str(exc), exit_code=getattr(exc,'returncode',None) or exit_code). Verified with .venv/bin/python that subprocess.TimeoutExpired has no `returncode` attribute (getattr → None) and that `None or 0` evaluates to 0, so the reported exit_code really is the 0 already in state. Looked for an existing test pinning this: none in tests/unit/test_steps covers the container stats probe raising. Tried to argue the trigger is unreachable: a stopped container or a dead daemon makes `docker exec` exit non-zero quickly (found=False, no raise), so the trigger is specifically a docker CLI that hangs >30 s (wedged Docker Desktop / unresponsive socket) or an OSError on the binary path — narrower than the auditor implies, which is why I set medium rather than high.
corrected_summary: In container mode check() writes state['exit_code'] = 0 at run_simulation.py:341 and then calls subprocess.run([docker,'exec',container,'test','-f',stats_path], timeout=30) at :349 with no try/except, so a TimeoutExpired or OSError escapes check() → _poll_step (no handler) → execute()'s generic `except Exception`, and a simulation that exited 0 is reported as StepFailed with the nonsensical exit_code 0. The same unguarded pattern also exists on the startup side at run_simulation.py:230-233 (the container `mkdir -p` probe), where a TimeoutExpired or a FileNotFoundError from an explicit-but-wrong `docker` path escapes as a raw StepFailed; that one is less harmful because the step genuinely could not start. Both contrast with collect_results.py:207-303 and ensure_container.py:217-316, which wrap everything.
failure_scenario: A 6-hour containerised gem5 run exits 0. On the next poll, check() reaps it, writes state['exit_code']=0, then the `docker exec <c> test -f <m5out>/stats.txt` probe hits a wedged Docker Desktop daemon and blocks past 30 s. subprocess.TimeoutExpired propagates out of check() into execute()'s handler, which sends StepFailed(error="Command '[...docker exec...]' timed out after 30 seconds", exit_code=0). Six hours of work is marked failed, the chained gem5_collect_results never runs, and the m5out data is never uploaded — while the step's own AI Note at :321-323 says a missing stats.txt must NOT fail the step.
fix: Wrap the probe in `try: ... except (subprocess.SubprocessError, OSError): found = False` so a failed probe means 'stats not found' (stats_artifact_id stays None) instead of deciding the step's fate; do the same for the container mkdir at :230-233, returning an error state rather than raising.

title: Raw /api/admin/* fetches bypass the global 401 handler -> an expired session renders empty admin tables instead of redirecting to /login
refutation_attempt: I checked whether the 401 handling exists anywhere upstream of these calls: client.ts:104-108 is the only place `setToken(null)` + `window.location.href = "/login"` lives, and `fetchUsers`/`fetchGroups` use bare `window.fetch`, not `api.request`, so they cannot reach it. I checked whether a non-OK response is distinguished: Admin.tsx:158 `if (res.ok)` then 162-166 `catch {} finally { setIsLoading(false) }` — previous (empty) state survives and the spinner stops, exactly as claimed. Admin.test.tsx:402-410 (403) and 413-421 (thrown) pin "No users found.", and all 159 tests in the three files pass (`npx vitest run` -> 159 passed). The one thing the auditor got wrong is the framing: this is not a rare expired-session case. I enumerated the server's real route table (`create_app()` -> app.routes) and there is NO /api/admin/* route at all, so this failure branch is taken on EVERY page load, 100% of the time. So the finding is confirmed, but as the mask over a much larger defect (reported separately) rather than as a session-expiry edge case.
corrected_summary: `fetchUsers` (Admin.tsx:150-167) and `fetchGroups` (529-539) hand-roll `fetch()` with an Authorization header read from localStorage, so they skip `request()`'s 401 -> clear-token -> /login behaviour and its `detail` extraction; any non-OK status leaves the previous (empty) state and stops the spinner, making 401/403/404/network-down all render as "No users found." / "No groups created yet."

title: useWebSocket unmount cleanup leaves a self-reconnecting orphan socket -> duplicated live-log lines
refutation_attempt: I looked for the guard: there is no `unmounted` ref, no generation counter, and `ws.onclose` is not nulled before `close()` - cleanup (lines 127-130) is exactly `clearTimeout(reconnectTimeout.current); wsRef.current?.close()`, and `onclose` (104-109) unconditionally schedules `connect()` (107), which constructs a new WebSocket and reassigns `wsRef.current` (78-79) with nothing left to close it. I checked whether the test suite already covers it: useWebSocket.test.tsx:507-523 fires `close` *before* unmount so the timer is pending and gets cleared - and the fake's `close = vi.fn()` (line 92) never invokes `onclose`, so the post-cleanup reconnect is unobservable in the suite. The only way to refute would be if a real `close()` never fired a close event; it does (for an OPEN socket after the closing handshake, and for a CONNECTING socket as the classic "WebSocket is closed before the connection is established" 1006 close). Could not refute.
corrected_summary: Cleanup cancels the pending timer and then calls `close()`, but the socket's own `onclose` fires after cleanup has returned and schedules a fresh `connect()`; that socket belongs to an unmounted component, is never closed, and re-reconnects on every close - so each mount/unmount cycle permanently adds one extra live dashboard socket.
failure_scenario: Production: click logout -> Layout unmounts (Layout.tsx:174-175) -> cleanup closes socket A -> A's onclose fires ~immediately and schedules a 1s timer -> socket B is created with no owner and stays connected forever. Log back in -> Layout mounts socket C. Now two sockets deliver every /ws/dashboard frame to the same module-level handleWsMessage, so useLiveLogsStore.appendLog pushes each step.log line twice and JobDetail's live log shows every output line duplicated; each further logout/login adds another duplicate. Dev is worse: StrictMode's double-invoked effect (main.tsx:31-35) produces the same orphan on first mount, so every dev session runs with doubled log lines.
fix: Add an `unmounted`/generation ref: set it in the cleanup before `close()` and bail out of `onclose` (and of `connect`) when set - or simply `ws.onclose = null` before `close()` in the cleanup. Also make FakeWebSocket.close() fire `onclose` so the test can see the regression.

corrected_summary: add_nodes_to_pool loops over node_ids calling ops.add_node_to_pool, which documents (ops.py:731-736) that a duplicate (pool_id, node_id) raises IntegrityError against the composite PK and does not upsert. The route's own note (pools.py:257, 262-266) is doubly wrong: it says "Retrying the same request is safe" and predicts that a duplicate "inserts a second PoolNodeMembership row unless the DB has a unique constraint" — the constraint exists (models.py:301-306), so the real outcome is a crash, not a duplicate row.
failure_scenario: POST /api/pools/{P}/nodes with body ["<N>", "<N>"] (same id twice), or any retry of a partially-succeeded batch as the docstring invites: the first ops.add_node_to_pool commits, the second raises sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError (UNIQUE constraint failed: pool_node_memberships.pool_id, pool_node_memberships.node_id) -> unhandled -> 500, with the earlier nodes already linked. Also hit by two operators adding the same node concurrently (the UI filters existing members, so it is the API/race path, not the happy path).
fix: Make the add idempotent: SELECT the membership first and skip it, or catch IntegrityError per node and treat it as already-a-member (return it in `added` or a separate `skipped` list). Then correct the pools.py:257 and 262-266 notes.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: Unique-name collisions on create endpoints surface as unhandled 500s instead of 409
corrected_summary: pools.name, credentials.name and storage_backends.name are all unique=True (models.py:276, 375, 418), and ops.create_pool/create_credential/create_storage_backend document that duplicates raise IntegrityError. None of the three routes pre-checks the name or catches IntegrityError (pools.py:134; credentials.py:39-51 catches only KeyError/ValueError; storage.py:164 checks only the credential's existence), and main.py declares no exception handler — so a duplicate name produces a 500. The auth route flagged exactly this hazard for usernames (auth.py:163-166) and handles it with a 409 pre-check; the pool/credential/backend routes did not get the same treatment.
failure_scenario: An operator creates credential "gem5-ssh", then re-submits the form (or a second admin creates the same name): mgr.store -> ops.create_credential -> sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError "UNIQUE constraint failed: credentials.name" escapes credentials.py:42-51 (which only maps KeyError/ValueError) -> HTTP 500 "Internal Server Error" with no indication that the name is taken. Same for POST /api/pools with an existing pool name (pools.py:134) and POST /api/storage/backends with an existing backend name.
fix: Mirror auth.py:163-166: pre-check the name (get_pool_by_name/get_credential_by_name/list_storage_backends) and raise 409 with a clear detail, and/or wrap the create in `except IntegrityError` -> 409 so the concurrent case is also covered.

title: A pre-restart step completion is consumed as the result of the re-dispatched step at the same index
refutation_attempt: The mechanism is real and I reproduced it: I drove _execute_remote_step to the point where its Event is registered, then called on_step_completed(str(job.id), 0, outputs={'stdout_from':'PRE-RESTART RUN'}) as an orphaned execution would, and the coroutine returned that foreign result with node_label attached. I also checked whether an existing test pins the safe behaviour — test_remote_step_timed_out_then_late_completion_is_discarded (test_runner_resume.py:1364) only covers the no-waiter case, so nothing contradicts this. But I did refute the auditor's headline scenario: on the restart path the re-dispatch cannot consume the orphan frame today, because (finding 2) the resumed remote step fails at placement/send before the orphan can arrive, and the finally at runner.py:761-762 then reaps the key. Reachability today is limited to a re-visit of the same index while an earlier visit's execution is still alive: a step that hits the 7200 s ceiling under on_fail="continue" followed by a backward jump to that index, or a duplicated critical frame colliding with such a re-visit. I also verified the two AI Notes the auditor calls false really do overclaim (runner.py:263-267 'nothing consumes it'; runner.py:755-762 'guarantees a late/duplicate agent message ... cannot be mistaken for the result of a future step that reuses the same job_id:step_index').
corrected_summary: The completion key is position-scoped ("{job_id}:{step_index}") rather than execution-scoped, so a frame produced by an abandoned earlier execution of the same index wakes and is recorded as the result of the current dispatch. Verified experimentally. Reachable today only via a 2h-timeout (or otherwise abandoned) execution plus a jump back to the same index — the restart scenario the auditor leads with is currently masked by finding 2 — but it becomes live the moment finding 2 is fixed, and two AI Notes already claim it cannot happen.
failure_scenario: Step 5 exceeds the 7200 s ceiling; the runner fails it, the orphan keeps running on the node, on_fail="continue" lets step 6 (jump target_step=5 on="fail") send the pointer back to 5. Index 5 is re-dispatched and its Event registered; the orphan then finishes and sends step.completed for job:5. The new wait is woken with the orphan's outputs, StepRun 5 is written 'success', those stale outputs are merged into context_data and persisted, and the newly dispatched execution keeps running unobserved on the node (double side effects, plus an unconsumed entry left in _step_results).
fix: Make the key execution-scoped: put the StepRun UUID (or a per-dispatch nonce) into ExecuteStepCommand, have the agent echo it in StepCompleted/StepFailed, key _step_events/_step_results on it, and drop frames whose token does not match the live dispatch. Until then, correct the two AI Notes at runner.py:263-267 and 755-762, which currently assert the guarantee this code does not provide.

title: Every local failure of a remote step is logged as running "on control-plane"
refutation_attempt: Verified the default and all four early returns by reading the file end to end: runner.py:414 defaults node_label to 'control-plane'; the no-node return (677-680), the credential return (710), the not-connected return (737) and the timeout return (754) all carry only status+error, and node_label is set only at runner.py:750 on the agent-reported path. Checked whether _format_log_block or the UI recovers the node from elsewhere — it does not; _format_log_block(idx, step_name, node_label, ...) at runner.py:91 renders whatever string it is handed, and the log is the plain text the Job Detail terminal shows. Confirmed by the existing test's expected banner shape (test_runner_resume.py:281-283). No behaviour is broken by this, which is why I hold it at low: it is a misleading operator-facing log line, not a wrong execution outcome.
corrected_summary: All four local-failure returns in _execute_remote_step omit node_label, so runner.py:414's fallback records a node-bound step's failure in the operator's terminal log as having run 'on control-plane' — and for the not-connected and timeout cases the node identity is known and would be the single most useful field. Impact is a confusing log line only; the auditor's severity of medium is inflated.
failure_scenario: A job pins target_os="linux" while only a macOS node is online. Job.log_text gets `===== [step 0] run_command on control-plane =====` followed by `error: No available node for step 'run_command' (os=linux)`, telling the operator a shell command ran in the server process. Same mislabelling for "Credential 'x' not found", "Agent for node <host> not connected" and "Step execution timed out (2h)".
fix: Set node_label on the remote path's failure dicts — "unplaced" for the no-node case and node.hostname for the credential/not-connected/timeout cases, where `node` is already bound — or have _run_job derive the label from the StepRun's node_id instead of defaulting to control-plane for a step whose class has REQUIRES_NODE=True.

title: _run_job overwrites Job.started_at on every resume
refutation_attempt: Checked whether the write is guarded or absorbed. runner.py:352-353 is unconditional and sits four lines after the get_job_by_id that already loaded the existing value; ops.update_job (ops.py:928-936) does a blind setattr after _sid_kwargs, so the column is genuinely overwritten. Reproduced: a job with started_at=2020-01-01 resumed through resume_active_jobs came back with started_at=2026-08-11. Then checked whether anything consumes it — Jobs.tsx:318 renders formatDuration(job.started_at, job.completed_at) and JobDetail.tsx:714-715 renders 'Started <relative>', so the corruption is user-visible. Severity stays low: per-step StepRun timestamps preserve the real forensic trail and no execution decision depends on the field.
corrected_summary: The unconditional update_job(status="running", started_at=now()) at the top of _run_job also runs on the resume path, replacing a resumed job's original start timestamp with the restart time and permanently under-reporting its duration.
failure_scenario: A 6-hour job starts at 10:00; the server restarts at 12:00 and resume_active_jobs re-adopts it. started_at becomes 12:00, so the Jobs list duration and the Job Detail 'Started X ago' label under-report by two hours for the rest of the job's life, and the original value is gone.
fix: Stamp it only on first entry: the job row is already loaded at runner.py:348, so pass started_at only when job.started_at is None.

title: get_step() is resolved twice per remote step and find_node_for_step's documented KeyError is unreachable
refutation_attempt: The factual claims hold: runner.py:374 resolves step_cls, runner.py:404-410 passes both step_cls and step_name into _execute_remote_step, runner.py:658-663 forwards only the name, and scheduler.py:82 resolves it again; scheduler.py:76-80's `Raises: KeyError` can therefore never fire from its only caller. I then pressed on the impact, because duplication alone is not a defect. get_step raises KeyError, and str(KeyError("Unknown step 'x'. Available: []")) is the repr, so Job.error would indeed be double-quoted; and because line 374 sits inside _run_job's outer try, the whole job fails regardless of that step's on_fail="continue". But reaching it requires a job persisted with a name the running build no longer registers (submit_job rejects unknown names at 400, and there is no route that inserts steps_config without validation), so this is a build-skew-only path with a cosmetic symptom. That is why I keep it low and describe it as hygiene plus a false docstring clause rather than a bug.
corrected_summary: The step class is resolved twice per remote step and the scheduler's documented KeyError contract is dead code from its only caller; the practical consequence is confined to a build-skew case where the failure surfaces as a whole-job failure (bypassing that step's on_fail policy) with a repr-quoted error string.
failure_scenario: A server build that no longer registers 'gem5_run_simulation' starts with a queued job that uses it. get_step raises at runner.py:374 inside _run_job's try, so the outer handler writes Job.status='failed' with error='"Unknown step \'gem5_run_simulation\'. Available: [...]"' — quoted, whole-job rather than per-step, and the scheduler branch documented to handle exactly this never runs.
fix: Pass the already-resolved step_cls into find_node_for_step, drop the second get_step and the now-false Raises clause. Optionally wrap runner.py:374 in try/except KeyError and convert it into a {"status":"failed","error":...} result so on_fail policy still applies.

title: Job submission applies no pool ACL, contradicting two docstrings that claim it does; require_pool_access is dead code
refutation_attempt: Verified the factual core and then attacked the severity. `grep -rn check_user_pool_access packages/` returns only the definition (ops.py:448), four docstring mentions, and the single call at deps.py:297 inside `require_pool_access`; `grep -rn require_pool_access` shows it is referenced only in docstrings/comments and never used as a FastAPI dependency. jobs.submit_job (jobs.py:227-279) contains no pool or node authorization. Verified live: regular user alice submits with `target_pool_id` = an admin-created pool she has zero GroupPoolAccess grants for -> 201. So deps.py:275-276 ('pool authorization is enforced ad hoc in the job routes instead') and ops.py:806-807 ('after the route has ... checked pool access') are both false. I downgrade severity because there is currently no way for an operator to *create* a grant and thus be misled into thinking a pool is restricted — there is no admin router (see that finding) and pools.py:26 already states plainly that any logged-in user can move nodes between pools. So today this is dead code plus two lying docstrings, not an exploitable bypass of a configured restriction.
corrected_summary: The entire Group -> GroupPoolAccess -> Pool ACL model has no enforcement point in the API: `ops.check_user_pool_access` is called only from the never-mounted `require_pool_access` factory, and jobs.submit_job performs no pool check. Two docstrings (deps.py:275-276 and ops.py:806-807) assert the opposite. Real severity is low rather than medium today, because no route exists to create a GroupPoolAccess grant in the first place, so no operator can believe a pool is restricted; the danger is entirely in the misleading documentation for whoever adds restricted pools next.
failure_scenario: Regular user alice (member of no group) POSTs /api/jobs with `target_pool_id` set to a pool she has no grant for -> 201 Created, and the scheduler places her steps on that pool's nodes (find_node_for_step filters only on status/OS). Verified: 201. The reader-facing failure is that a future maintainer adding a restricted pool trusts deps.py:276/ops.py:807 and adds no check.
fix: Either enforce it — in submit_job, when `body.target_pool_id` (or any step's `target_pool_id`) is set, call `await ops.check_user_pool_access(db, user.id, pool_id)` and 403 otherwise — or delete `require_pool_access` and correct deps.py:273-278 and ops.py:806-808 to state that pool ACLs are unenforced.

title: Results-manifest error handler misses EOFError, so a truncated tarball yields a bare 500 instead of the documented detail
refutation_attempt: Checked whether EOFError is reachable and whether it is already covered. `EOFError` inherits directly from `Exception` (MRO: EOFError -> Exception -> BaseException), so it is caught by neither `tarfile.TarError` nor `OSError`. Reproduced: a real .tar.gz truncated to half its bytes makes `tarfile.open(path, "r:gz")`/`getmembers()` raise EOFError, and through the app `GET /api/jobs/{id}/results/manifest` returns 500 with body 'Internal Server Error' (no `detail`), whereas non-gzip garbage correctly returns 500 `{"detail":"Could not read archive: not a gzip file"}`. The docstring at jobs.py:437-439 explicitly promises the detail for 'truncated upload', and the upload AI Note at jobs.py:371-375 names the exact scenario. I downgrade severity: both branches are 500s, so the real impact is a missing error message, not a wrong result or data loss.
corrected_summary: `except (tarfile.TarError, OSError)` does not cover `EOFError`, which is what a valid-gzip-header-but-truncated stream raises — precisely the corruption this handler's own docstring says it exists to report. Impact is a bare 500 with no `detail` instead of the documented message, so low rather than medium.
failure_scenario: An agent's `PUT /api/jobs/{id}/results` upload is cut mid-stream (the route writes straight to the final path with no temp+rename, jobs.py:376-379), leaving a truncated results.tar.gz. `has_results` is True, so the Job Detail page requests the manifest and gets `500 'Internal Server Error'` with an empty detail; ResultsTree can show no reason and the operator gets no hint that the archive is truncated. A wholly non-gzip file is handled correctly, which makes the failure mode look inconsistent.
fix: Broaden to `except (tarfile.TarError, OSError, EOFError, zlib.error) as exc:` and add `from exc`. Better still, make uploads atomic (write `results.tar.gz.part`, then `os.replace`) so truncated archives never become visible.

title: Any authenticated user can cancel or delete any other user's job (no ownership check anywhere)
refutation_attempt: Verified the fact, then argued severity down. Confirmed live: a regular-user bearer token deletes a job whose `submitted_by` is the admin -> 204, and cancels one -> 200 with status 'cancelled'. `ops.list_jobs` does expose a `submitted_by` filter (ops.py:867) that no route passes. Against the finding: this is author-flagged three times (jobs.py:168-170, 534-535, 579-580) as a deliberate single-tenant assumption, and it is not an escalation beyond the project's stated trust model — any authenticated user can already submit a job that runs arbitrary shell on any node, which is strictly more powerful than cancelling someone else's job. The one genuine residual is destroying another user's job *record* (and reading their log/results), which the trust model does not obviously grant.
corrected_summary: cancel_job and delete_job gate on `CurrentUser` only and never compare `job.submitted_by` to `user.id`; nothing in this router does object-level authz (list/detail/log/results/manifest/download are global too). Confirmed, but low severity: it is documented three times as an accepted single-tenant assumption, and job-submission rights already imply shell access on every node, so the only real delta is cross-user record deletion and log/result disclosure.
failure_scenario: Non-admin alice calls `POST /api/jobs/{bob_job_id}/cancel` on bob's long gem5 run -> 200 and the job is marked cancelled (the agent keeps burning the node per the AI Note at jobs.py:547-550), then `DELETE /api/jobs/{bob_job_id}` -> 204, destroying his record; she can also read his full terminal log and download his results tarball. Verified 204/200 with a regular-user token against an admin-submitted job.
fix: If single-tenant is intended, state it once in the module docstring and drop the per-route notes. Otherwise add `if job.submitted_by != str(user.id) and user.role != "admin": raise HTTPException(403)` to cancel_job/delete_job, and scope list_jobs via the existing `ops.list_jobs(submitted_by=...)` parameter.

title: GET /api/jobs?limit=-1 disables pagination entirely (SQLite LIMIT -1 = unlimited)
refutation_attempt: Checked for bounds anywhere upstream or downstream: the handler declares plain `limit: int = 50` / `offset: int = 0` (jobs.py:141-142) with no `Query(...)`, and `ops.list_jobs` (ops.py:898) applies `.limit(limit).offset(offset)` with no clamping. Reproduced with 7 seeded jobs: `?limit=-1` -> 200 with all 7 (SQLite treats LIMIT -1 as unlimited), `?limit=3` -> 3, `?offset=-3` -> 200 with all 7 (silently ignored), `?limit=0` -> 0. Corrected the anchor: the defect is the parameter declarations at jobs.py:141-142, not the `ops.list_jobs` call at 176. Severity stays low — this is a trusted-LAN performance foot-gun the AI Note at 172-175 already half-anticipates.
corrected_summary: `limit` and `offset` carry no `Query(ge=..., le=...)` bounds, so besides the large-value case the author flagged, `?limit=-1` renders as `LIMIT -1` which SQLite treats as 'no limit' — any authenticated user defeats paging with one query-string character. `?offset=-3` is accepted and silently ignored rather than 422'd.
failure_scenario: With 7 jobs, `GET /api/jobs?limit=-1` returns all 7 (verified); on a cluster with tens of thousands of job rows the same request selects and Pydantic-serialises every row in one shot, blocking the event loop and inflating memory.
fix: Declare `limit: int = Query(50, ge=1, le=200)` and `offset: int = Query(0, ge=0)` so FastAPI 422s out-of-range values before the query runs, and extend the AI Note at 172-175 to mention the negative case.

title: deps.py AI Note documents 403 for a missing Authorization header; FastAPI 0.135 returns 401 and the test suite pins 401
refutation_attempt: Checked whether the note might be right for some header shape. It is not: with fastapi 0.135.3, `GET /api/auth/me`, `/api/jobs` and `/api/nodes` with no Authorization header all return `401 {"detail":"Not authenticated"}`, as do `Authorization: Basic zzz` and a bare `Authorization: Bearer`. tests/integration/test_auth_routes.py:432 (`test_register_unauthenticated_is_401`) pins 401 with the comment 'HTTPBearer with no Authorization header -> 401 Not authenticated', frontend/src/api/client.ts:104 branches on 401 only, and auth.py:194-197 correctly documents 401 — deps.py:60-65 is the lone outlier (a stale description of pre-0.10x HTTPBearer behaviour). Severity is low because the code is correct and only the comment is wrong; the 'failure' is a human misreading, not a runtime defect.
corrected_summary: The AI Note at deps.py:60-65 states that HTTPBearer rejects a missing/malformed header 'with 403' and warns about clients branching on 401 vs 403. On the pinned FastAPI (0.135.3) that rejection is 401 — which is also what the tests and the frontend assume — so the note documents the opposite of the real contract. Documentation-only defect.
failure_scenario: A developer reading deps.py:60-65 writes or reviews a client that treats 403 as 'not authenticated, redirect to login' and 401 as 'token semantically bad'. Every unauthenticated request actually returns `401 {"detail":"Not authenticated"}`, so their 403 branch is dead and unauthenticated requests fall through the wrong path; the note also misleads anyone auditing why client.ts handles only 401.
fix: Update the AI Note to say 401 (matching FastAPI >= 0.10x and tests/integration/test_auth_routes.py:432-439), or pin the intended code explicitly with a comment naming the version-dependent status.

title: reconnect's log can echo the node api_key, contradicting its "never re-disclosed" docstring
refutation_attempt: Tried to refute the reachability the auditor themselves called 'likely'. It turns out to be more reliable than claimed, not less: the *success* branch of INSTALL_SH (provisioner.py:228) also runs `tail -n 6 agent.log` after `sleep 3`, and every non-'WS_HOST ' stdout line is appended to `log` at provisioner.py:539 and returned in the 200 body of reconnect_node (nodes.py:521) — and Nodes.tsx:512-514 renders `done.log.join("\n")` in the reconnect dialog. `_start` truncates agent.log (`>agent.log`), and the agent's INFO-level startup emits exactly five lines: 'Nexus Agent ... starting', 'Server: ...', 'Connecting to ws://host:8000/ws/agent/<id>?api_key=<plaintext>&node_id=...' (connection.py:239 + _build_url at 297), 'Connected to server', 'Registered as ...'. All five fit inside `tail -n 6`, so the plaintext key lands in the response on the normal path, not just the AGENT_DIED/502 path (provisioner.py:230, `tail -n 25`). Default log level is INFO (main.py:90) and nexusctl redirects stdout+stderr into agent.log. Severity stays low: the consumer is an admin who is already SSH-ing to the box.
corrected_summary: reconnect_node's docstring (nodes.py:473-475) promises the response carries no api_key because 'the existing key is reused on the device and is never re-disclosed', but the provisioner streams the install script's stdout verbatim into `log`, and INSTALL_SH tails agent.log — which contains the agent's connect URL including `?api_key=<plaintext>`. Correction to the auditor: this happens on the *successful* 200 path via `tail -n 6` (provisioner.py:228), where the key is then rendered on screen by Nodes.tsx:514, as well as on the AGENT_DIED 502 path via `tail -n 25` (provisioner.py:230). Confidence is 'certain', not 'likely'.
failure_scenario: Admin calls `POST /api/nodes/{id}/reconnect` with default `service=false`. The installer starts the agent, sleeps 3s, sees it running, echoes AGENT_RUNNING and `tail -n 6 agent.log`; those lines include `Connecting to ws://host:8000/ws/agent/<node_id>?api_key=<plaintext>&node_id=...`. The provisioner appends them to `log`, the route returns them in the 200 body, and the Nodes page prints them in the reconnect dialog — so the key the endpoint promises never to re-disclose appears on screen and in any devtools/HAR capture.
fix: Redact the key from provisioner output before returning it (the value is already a parameter, so a `line.replace(api_key, "***")` pass over `log`/`error` suffices), or drop the 'never re-disclosed' claim from the docstring.

title: Duplicate name on pool / storage-backend / credential creation surfaces as an unhandled IntegrityError (HTTP 500)
refutation_attempt: I checked for an upstream guard: no pre-existence check in create_pool/update_pool/register_backend/create_credential; no `add_exception_handler`/`@app.exception_handler` anywhere in main.py or api/; PoolCreate/StorageBackendCreate/CredentialCreate have no uniqueness validators. I confirmed the constraints exist (models.py:276 pools.name unique, :375 credentials.name unique, :418 storage_backends.name unique) and reproduced all three through the real app: sqlite3.IntegrityError 'UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.name' / 'credentials.name' / 'storage_backends.name' escape the handlers (TestClient re-raises; under uvicorn this is a 500). I also checked for a bigger impact than a wrong status code — the failed session is request-scoped and closed by get_db, so there is no cross-request contamination and no partial write. That caps the real impact at 'wrong status code + opaque UI error', which is why I downgraded from medium.
corrected_summary: None of the create/update handlers for the three unique-named resources catches sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError and there is no app-level handler, so an ordinary duplicate-name entry returns 500 instead of 409/400. Real and easily triggered, but the operation is correctly rejected and nothing is corrupted — the defect is the status code and the useless error the UI can show.
failure_scenario: Reproduced: POST /api/pools {'name':'gpu'} twice -> the second raises 'UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.name' out of the handler -> 500. Same for POST /api/credentials with an existing name, POST /api/storage/backends with an existing backend name, and PUT /api/pools/{id} renaming onto an existing name (pools.py:197). The operator re-creating 'minio-primary' after a config mistake sees a generic server failure and cannot tell a name clash from a server fault.
fix: Catch sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError in these handlers and return 409 with the offending field, or register a single app-level IntegrityError handler in create_app. Update pools.py's AI Note at L130-133 to state the resulting status code.

title: Re-adding a node already in a pool raises IntegrityError -> HTTP 500 with earlier nodes already committed
refutation_attempt: The mechanism is real — I reproduced it: a second POST /api/pools/{id}/nodes with the same node_id raises 'UNIQUE constraint failed: pool_node_memberships.pool_id, pool_node_memberships.node_id' out of the route (composite PK at models.py:301-306; ops.add_node_to_pool commits per node and documents the raise at ops.py:731-735; the route has no try). But the auditor's failure scenario is REFUTED on three counts. (1) There is no multi-select 'Add' in the Pools UI: AddNodeDropdown adds exactly one node per click via api.addNodeToPool(poolId, nodeId) (Pools.tsx:292, client.ts:294), so 'earlier nodes already committed' cannot happen from the UI. (2) The UI cannot offer an existing member: Pools.tsx:278-280 filters candidates with `!existingNodeIds.has(n.id)`, and the docstring at L246-247 states the filter exists 'so a node can never be added twice'. (3) 'Retrying 500s forever, which reads as a permanently broken pool' is overstated — the node is already a member, so the pool is fine; the retry is simply redundant. Reachable only via direct API/CLI use, or a double-click racing a stale membership list. Also, the AI Note at L256-259 is conditional ('unless the DB has a unique constraint'), so 'describes the opposite behaviour' is unfair.
corrected_summary: add_nodes_to_pool loops over ops.add_node_to_pool, which commits per node and raises IntegrityError on the (pool_id, node_id) composite PK, and the route catches nothing — so a duplicate becomes an unhandled 500 (and, for a multi-node API request, leaves earlier nodes committed). The Pools UI cannot trigger this: it filters out existing members and posts one node at a time, so the reachable triggers are direct API/CLI calls and a double-click against a stale member list.
failure_scenario: Reproduced via the API: POST /api/pools/{id}/nodes with body ["<node-uuid>"], then repeat the identical request -> sqlite3.IntegrityError 'UNIQUE constraint failed: pool_node_memberships.pool_id, pool_node_memberships.node_id' escapes the handler (500 under uvicorn). For a multi-node body [A(already a member), B], A raises first and B is never added, while any node earlier in the list is already committed.
fix: Skip nodes already in the pool (membership check, or catch IntegrityError per node and continue) and report them in a `skipped` list, or make ops.add_node_to_pool an upsert. Rewrite the AI Note at L256-259 to state what actually happens now that the constraint is known to exist.

title: Credential metadata cannot be changed without re-supplying the plaintext secret, and a placeholder secret silently destroys the real one
refutation_attempt: I reproduced all three responses against the real app: PUT with no `fields` -> 422 {'loc':['body','fields'],'msg':'Field required'}; PUT with fields={} -> 422 'Missing required field: token'; PUT with fields={'token':'PLACEHOLDER'} -> 200 and get_by_name then returns {'token':'PLACEHOLDER',...}. Confirmed the cause: CredentialCreate.fields (schemas.py:474) has no default, and update_credential passes body.fields to mgr.update_fields unconditionally, which re-validates and replaces encrypted_fields wholesale (manager.py:110-114). I then checked reachability, which is where the auditor overstates it: frontend/src/api/client.ts has no updateCredential at all (only list/create/delete/test), no page calls PUT /api/credentials/{id}, and tests/integration/test_credentials_routes.py has zero PUT tests. So no operator can hit this through the dashboard — it is a latent API-shape defect, not an operator footgun. Hence low, not medium.
corrected_summary: PUT /api/credentials/{id} reuses CredentialCreate (where `fields` is required) and always calls mgr.update_fields, so there is no metadata-only edit path and a placeholder secret silently overwrites the real, unrecoverable one. Latent: no client calls this route (client.ts has no updateCredential) and no test covers it. Additional wart in the same handler: the required `credential_type` in the body is silently ignored — update_fields validates against the *stored* type and ops.update_credential never writes credential_type — so changing a credential's type is impossible and fails with a misleading 'Missing required field' 422.

While there, either honour `credential_type` (re-validate and rewrite the column) or drop it from the update body so it cannot be silently ignored.

title: No route serves artifact bytes: artifacts.py and storage.py each name the other as the download owner, and the UI links to a nonexistent /api/artifacts/{id}/download
refutation_attempt: I enumerated the live routes on the real app instead of trusting the grep: the only artifact/storage paths are /api/artifacts, /api/storage/backends, /api/storage/backends/{backend_id}, /api/storage/backends/{backend_id}/health, /api/storage/transfer and /api/storage/transfers — there is no download route anywhere. Downloading is the storage layer's job (/api/storage/...)' while storage.py:26-27 says 'routes/artifacts.py serves the downloads'; ops.get_artifact_by_id's docstring adds a third claim ('Entry point for the download and results-manifest endpoints'). I confirmed latency: nothing outside services/storage/manager.py calls upload_artifact or ops.create_artifact — gem5_collect_results uses the separate results-tarball path (PUT to .nexus-results/), not Artifact rows — so GET /api/artifacts?job_id= always returns [] and the table never renders. corrected_summary: There is no GET /api/artifacts/{id}/download route (verified against the running app's route table: 404), yet JobDetail.tsx:966 renders a Download link to it and JobDetail.test.tsx pins that href. Three docstrings disagree about who owns artifact downloads: artifacts.py:10-11 points at /api/storage/..., storage.py:26-27 points back at routes/artifacts.py, and ops.get_artifact_by_id claims to be the download endpoint's entry point. refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.

title: Fernet InvalidToken stringifies to "" -> decrypt failures produce a diagnostic-free log line and an empty API error
refutation_attempt: I verified the premise rather than trusting it: `.venv/bin/python -c "from cryptography.fernet import InvalidToken; print(repr(str(InvalidToken())))"` prints `''`. I then traced the two consumers to confirm neither adds type information: storage/manager.py:119 `logger.error(f"Failed to initialize backend {backend_model.name}: {e}")` (f-string, not logger.exception, not %r) and routes/credentials.py:97-98 `except Exception as exc: return {"success": False, "error": str(exc)}`. I looked for a typed re-raise inside FieldEncryptor.decrypt (encryption.py:28-31) — there is none, the bare `self._fernet.decrypt(ciphertext)` propagates. I checked whether config.py already covers this: config.py:84-92 documents only the *missing*-key case (`Fernet("")` -> ValueError, which does have a message), not the wrong-key case. Not refuted, but this is diagnosability, not correctness.
corrected_summary: FieldEncryptor.decrypt lets cryptography's InvalidToken propagate, and `str(InvalidToken())` is the empty string, so every consumer that formats it with `{e}`/`str(exc)` emits a message with no content. Real but low severity: nothing computes a wrong result — the operator just gets a blank reason for a correctly-detected failure.
failure_scenario: An operator rotates CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY (or restores nexus.db from a backup taken under a different key) and restarts. init_backends -> _create_backend_instance -> CredentialManager.get -> FieldEncryptor.decrypt raises InvalidToken, caught at storage/manager.py:115 and logged as literally `Failed to initialize backend primary: `. Every backend disappears from the registry with no stated cause. Clicking Test on the same credential returns HTTP 200 `{"success": false, "error": ""}`, which the dashboard renders as a blank failure reason.
fix: Catch InvalidToken in FieldEncryptor.decrypt and re-raise typed: `raise ValueError("credential decryption failed - CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY does not match the stored ciphertext") from exc`. Independently switch storage/manager.py:119 to `logger.exception(...)` or `%r` so any empty-str exception still shows its type.

title: transfer_artifact has no source==destination guard; delete_source then deletes the only copy
refutation_attempt: I confirmed the code gap (manager.py:342-376 never compares `artifact.storage_backend_id` (line 349/357) with `dest_backend_id` (line 350/358); routes/storage.py:339-343 passes both through unguarded) and traced what would actually happen: base.stream_to (base.py:203-208) downloads key K to a temp file and re-uploads it to K on the same instance (a no-op overwrite), the row is marked completed at 369-373, then `source.delete(K)` at 375-376 unlinks it. So the defect is real. But I then tried hard to reach it and could not: TransferRequest.dest_backend_id is typed `UUID` (schemas.py:581), so the destination lookup at manager.py:358 hits the str/UUID keying miss and raises KeyError -> 404 *before* any bytes move, for every backend in a real deployment; and the artifacts table is empty in production because `ops.create_artifact` (ops.py:1395) is only called from manager.py:262 and `upload_artifact` has zero non-test callers (routes/artifacts.py only lists rows; job results go to a local tarball path in routes/jobs.py:321-414). Doubly latent, exactly as the auditor honestly stated — so I am downgrading severity, not refuting.
corrected_summary: transfer_artifact never rejects dest == source, so with delete_source=True it would copy an object onto itself and then delete it, leaving a 'completed' transfer row and an artifact row pointing at a key whose bytes are gone. Confirmed as a code defect but currently unreachable twice over: the UUID/str keying bug makes every destination lookup 404 first, and nothing in the server ever creates an artifact row. Severity low today; it becomes real silent data loss the moment the keying bug is fixed and artifact upload is wired up.
failure_scenario: Once the keying bug is fixed and uploads are wired: a user posts `{"artifact_id": X, "dest_backend_id": <the backend X already lives on>, "delete_source": true}` to /api/storage/transfer (easy mis-click — the dashboard's destination dropdown is not filtered against the artifact's current backend). stream_to copies K from B to a temp file and back to K on B, the transfer row is marked completed, `source.delete(K)` removes the object, and artifact.storage_backend_id is repointed to the same B — the row looks healthy, the bytes are gone, and the audit trail says 'completed'.
fix: Reject up front, before creating the transfer row: `if str(artifact.storage_backend_id) == str(dest_backend_id): raise ValueError("source and destination backend are the same")` (routes/storage.py already maps ValueError-class failures usefully), and/or skip the delete when source is dest.

title: transfer_artifact's failure handler reuses a session that may need rollback, masking the real error
refutation_attempt: I reproduced the mechanism instead of arguing about it. Using the repo's own models/ops against sqlite+aiosqlite in-memory: create a StorageTransfer, force a failing commit, then call `ops.update_transfer` on the same session -> `PendingRollbackError: This Session's transaction has been rolled back due to a previous exception during flush. To begin a new transaction with this Session, first issue Session.rollback().` So the handler at manager.py:391-398 does replace the original exception whenever the failure came from `await db.commit()` at line 389. I checked whether ops.update_transfer avoids the poisoned session — it does not: ops.py:1513 `db.get(StorageTransfer, _sid(transfer_id))` then `await db.commit()`, both illegal in that state. I checked whether the handler is unreachable for a commit failure specifically: line 389 flushes a plain str assignment, so the realistic triggers are SQLite 'database is locked' under concurrent writes or a disk-full OperationalError — plausible, not contrived. One auditor detail is wrong and corrected below.
corrected_summary: The `except` block at manager.py:391 issues another DB write on the same session without rolling back first, so a failure originating from `await db.commit()` (line 389) makes ops.update_transfer raise PendingRollbackError in place of the real error, leaving the transfer row stuck at 'completed'. Correction: the auditor wrote that 'routes/storage.py catches neither KeyError nor RuntimeError' — it catches both (lines 344-347); the reason the operator gets an opaque 500 is that PendingRollbackError is a sqlalchemy InvalidRequestError, which is neither. Severity low because the surrounding transfer path is itself unreachable in production today.
failure_scenario: A transfer copies the object, the row is marked 'completed' (369-373), delete_source runs, then `await db.commit()` at 389 fails (SQLite 'database is locked' under a concurrent write, or disk full). Control enters the except at 391; `ops.update_transfer` -> `db.get(...)` raises PendingRollbackError (reproduced), which propagates out of transfer_artifact instead of the real OperationalError. routes/storage.py catches KeyError/RuntimeError only, so the client gets a 500 naming the wrong error, the transfer row still says 'completed', and the artifact row still points at the (now emptied, if delete_source was set) source backend.
fix: Start the handler with `await db.rollback()` before ops.update_transfer, and chain the original exception into the recorded error text (`error=f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"`).

title: S3Strategy builds endpoint_url by blind string concatenation and uses bare truthiness for use_ssl
refutation_attempt: I tested the auditor's mechanism rather than accepting it, and two details are wrong. (a) `boto3.client('s3', endpoint_url='http://https://minio.lab:9000', ...)` does NOT raise — I ran it and the client constructs fine, reporting that endpoint verbatim. The failure surfaces one line later, from `MinIOBackend._ensure_bucket`'s head_bucket/create_bucket (minio_backend.py:69, 85-88), and init_backends DOES log it (manager.py:119), so the case is not 'near-silent' the way the auditor framed it — though the message can be actively misleading (on my box head_bucket against that mangled URL returned a ClientError 403 Forbidden, which reads as a credentials problem, not a malformed endpoint). (b) I did confirm the input side: validate() (lines 11-14) only checks presence/non-emptiness, serialize() (line 22) stores `use_ssl` completely uncoerced, get_client_config (line 27) selects the scheme with bare truthiness, `use_ssl` is advertised as an optional field with no type metadata (line 46), and the dashboard renders every required/optional field as a plain text input writing `e.target.value` (frontend/src/pages/Admin.tsx:1250-1299) — so a string is the only thing that path can ever send. Confirmed, at low severity.
corrected_summary: S3Strategy prefixes a scheme onto whatever `endpoint` was stored and picks it with `if decrypted_fields.get('use_ssl')`, and neither validate() nor serialize() normalizes either field. The genuinely wrong outcome is the use_ssl one: because the dashboard sends all optional fields as strings, `use_ssl: "false"` is truthy and selects https. The endpoint-with-scheme case is real but louder than claimed — boto3 accepts the mangled URL, and the backend fails at bucket-ensure time with a logged (if misleading) error rather than silently.
failure_scenario: (b) An operator fills the `use_ssl` optional text input with `false`. serialize stores the string verbatim; get_client_config sees a truthy value and emits `endpoint_url="https://minio.lab:9000"`; boto3 attempts TLS against a plain-HTTP MinIO and every operation fails, with the credential's own metadata reading `use_ssl: false`. (a) An operator types `https://minio.lab:9000` into the endpoint field; get_client_config emits `endpoint_url="http://https://minio.lab:9000"`, MinIOBackend construction fails inside _ensure_bucket, init_backends logs and skips the backend, and — because the health route is separately always-broken (finding 3) — the dashboard shows the same red dot it would for a real outage.
fix: In S3Strategy.serialize, urlparse `endpoint`: if a scheme is present, derive use_ssl from it and store only the netloc; and coerce use_ssl with an explicit parser treating "false"/"0"/"no"/"" as False. Longer term, give optional_fields() type metadata so the dashboard can render a checkbox instead of a text input.

title: server_hostname() does not filter localhost.localdomain despite its docstring's stated rule
refutation_attempt: The code fact is exactly as claimed — provisioner.py:318 is `if not h or h in ("localhost", "localhost.local"):`, an exact-match tuple, while the docstring at 306-312 promises None 'whenever gethostname() returned a loopback name that a remote agent could never resolve back to this machine'; tests/unit/test_provisioner.py:619-628 pins the pass-through. But I could not sustain the stated *impact*, and it is worth correcting because the auditor inherited it from that test's own docstring: the installer probes candidates with `asyncio.wait_for(websockets.connect(...), timeout=6)` (INSTALL_SH lines 141-146), and on the device `localhost.localdomain` resolves via /etc/hosts to 127.0.0.1 (the RHEL default hosts line lists it), so the probe fails with an immediate ECONNREFUSED, not a 6-second timeout. If the name does not resolve at all, the failure is likewise immediate. A 6s stall would require DNS itself to black-hole the name. So the real cost is one fast-failing connection attempt, i.e. negligible.
corrected_summary: The loopback guard is an exact-match tuple, so the common RHEL/CentOS/Fedora default `localhost.localdomain` passes through and is returned as the highest-priority callback candidate, contradicting the function's own documented rule. Real but cosmetic: the '6 seconds slower per provisioning run' cost claimed by both the auditor and the pinning test is wrong — the name resolves to loopback on the device, so the probe fails immediately with ECONNREFUSED and the wasted work is one fast round trip, not a timeout.
failure_scenario: Nexus server runs on a RHEL box whose hostname was never set, so gethostname() returns 'localhost.localdomain'. callback_candidates() returns it first, provision() passes it as the first CANDS entry, and the installer's probe attempts and fails a useless connection to the device's own loopback before falling through to the IP candidates. The residual (rare) risk is selecting an address that can never reach the server if something on the device happens to answer a WebSocket handshake on that port.
fix: Match the loopback family rather than two literals: reject when the name is `localhost` or starts with `localhost.` — or, more robustly, when `socket.gethostbyname(h)` lands in 127.0.0.0/8. Then update test_server_hostname_accepts_localhost_localdomain to expect None and drop its incorrect 'costs one handshake timeout' rationale.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: Non-string credential field values crash strategy.serialize() -> HTTP 500 instead of 422
corrected_summary: `CredentialCreate.fields` is an untyped `dict` (schemas.py:468), and every strategy's `serialize()` calls `.strip()` on the raw values (S3 lines 18-21, GitPAT 62-63, GitSSH 104, SMB 170-172, Basic 207) while `validate()` only checks truthiness. A JSON client that sends a number or boolean where a string is expected passes validate() and then raises AttributeError inside serialize(). routes/credentials.py:48-51 catches only KeyError (400) and ValueError (422), so the AttributeError escapes as a 500.
failure_scenario: POST /api/credentials with `{"name":"x","credential_type":"basic","fields":{"username":123,"password":"p"}}`. I reproduced it against the real manager: `mgr.store(..., credential_type='basic', fields={'username':123,'password':'p'})` raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'strip'`. Because the route maps only KeyError/ValueError, the client receives a 500 Internal Server Error (and a stack trace in the server log) for what is plainly a malformed request body — the same class of input the neighbouring 422 paths handle cleanly.
fix: Either type the wire contract (`fields: dict[str, str]` on CredentialCreate, so Pydantic rejects with 422 before the manager is reached) or coerce/validate inside each strategy's validate(): `if not isinstance(raw_fields.get(f), str): raise ValueError(f"field {f} must be a string")`.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: Duplicate credential name raises IntegrityError -> HTTP 500 instead of 409/422
corrected_summary: `credentials.name` is UNIQUE (models.py:376) but neither CredentialManager.store (manager.py:63-68) nor ops.create_credential (ops.py:1169-1176) checks for an existing name, and routes/credentials.py:48-51 catches only KeyError/ValueError, so SQLAlchemy's IntegrityError propagates as a 500. The frontend clearly expects a clean error here — Admin.test.tsx:1453 mocks the rejection as `new Error("Credential name in use")` — so the intended contract is a 4xx.
failure_scenario: Two operators (or one operator retrying after a network hiccup) POST /api/credentials with the same `name`. I reproduced it against the real manager: the second `mgr.store(db, name="dup", ...)` raises `sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (sqlite3.IntegrityError) UNIQUE constraint failed: credentials.name`. Neither the manager nor the route handles it, so the client gets an opaque 500 with a stack trace instead of a 409/422 telling them the name is taken.
