title: Output line longer than 64 KiB raises ValueError, fails the step, and leaves the child process hung and unreachable by cancel()
refutation_attempt: The mechanism reproduces end-to-end through the real StepExecutor: a synthetic step returning {"command": "...300 KB with no newline; sleep..."} produced step.started then step.failed with error 'Separator is not found, and chunk exceed the limit' (raised at executor.py:413 via asyncio/streams.py:571), the sibling stream_pipe coroutine was still pending afterwards, process.wait()/kill() never ran, execute()'s finally popped _running_steps, and `ps` showed the child still alive both immediately after and 2s after the interpreter exited. BUT I refuted the auditor's trigger and severity: run_command is not a subprocess step. An AST scan of all 13 shipped steps shows none emits a "command" key in startup() state, and shell/run_command.py:23, shell/run_script.py:23 and python/run.py:28 explicitly document that they deliberately do not — they Popen to temp files and poll with waitpid. `if "command" in state` (executor.py:206) is therefore never true today, so _run_subprocess, stream_pipe, and adapter.shell_command()/temp_dir() are all unreachable from shipped steps. The docstring at 406-408 is nonetheless wrong (readline() does have a 64 KiB limit).
corrected_summary: asyncio.create_subprocess_shell gives each StreamReader a 64 KiB limit, so pipe.readline() at line 413 raises ValueError on any output run of >64 KiB without a newline; the exception aborts the gather before process.wait(), leaves the sibling reader task pending, never kills the child, and the finally pops _running_steps so nothing can reach the process again. The AI Note at 406-408 asserts the opposite ("readline() has no length limit"). Latent only: no shipped step puts a "command" key in startup() state, so _run_subprocess is currently dead code — the auditor's run_command/docker-pull trigger is wrong, since run_command is a poll step writing to temp files.
failure_scenario: Someone adds a step that uses the documented simple shape (startup() returns {"command": "..."}) — the same shape tests/unit/test_agent.py:803 exercises with _CommandStep. Its command emits a single >64 KiB run without a newline (e.g. `base64 -w0 bigfile`, a minified JSON body from curl, or accumulated \r progress output). readline() raises ValueError, the step is reported FAILED with 'Separator is not found, and chunk exceed the limit' even though the command was healthy, stdout/stderr in the job log are truncated at that point, and the child is left blocked in write() on an undrained pipe with no way for cancel() to reach it (verified: the child outlived the agent interpreter).
fix: Read with a bounded reader instead of readline() — `chunk = await pipe.read(65536)` and split on newlines yourself, or pass a large `limit=` to create_subprocess_shell and catch ValueError per line. Independently wrap the gather in try/finally that terminate()/kill()s and awaits the process so no failure path leaks a child, and correct the AI Note at 406-408.

title: POSSIBLE BUG confirmed: unreadable /etc/os-release either flaps the node online/offline forever or kills the agent process
refutation_attempt: Traced the whole propagation path looking for a guard and found none: _detect_os_version() is called bare inside detect_capabilities()'s dict literal (capability.py:63), _send_registration() has no try (connection.py:317), and _connect_and_run() awaits it inside the `async with` without a handler (connection.py:251). Class hierarchy settles the split: PermissionError/IsADirectoryError are OSError (in run()'s tuple at line 129 → infinite retry) while UnicodeDecodeError is a ValueError (not in the tuple → process death, matching the behaviour pinned by test_run_lets_unexpected_exceptions_escape). The flap claim also holds: ws.py sets status=online and broadcasts at accept time, before the agent's register arrives, so each failed registration produces an online→offline pair. No test covers os-release. What I do push back on is likelihood: /etc/os-release is world-readable by convention and Python's C-locale coercion means UTF-8 decoding, so both triggers need an unusual host (hardened container, or vendor branding written in a non-UTF-8 encoding).
corrected_summary: _detect_os_version()'s /etc/os-release parser guards only FileNotFoundError, so any other read failure aborts registration: OSError subclasses (PermissionError, IsADirectoryError) are absorbed by run()'s retry tuple and produce an endless non-registering online/offline flap, while UnicodeDecodeError (a ValueError) escapes run() and kills the agent. This violates the module's own design constraint at capability.py:18-20 that every probe degrade rather than raise; author-flagged at capability.py:110-113.
failure_scenario: On a hardened/confined Linux node where open("/etc/os-release") raises PermissionError, the agent connects, the server marks the node online and broadcasts it (ws.py:308), then _send_registration() raises before the register frame is sent. _connect_and_run unwinds, the socket closes, the server marks the node offline and broadcasts again, and run() absorbs the OSError and retries — forever, at 1s→2s→…→60s. The node never records os_type/arch/ram, can never be scheduled, and spams dashboard status transitions. If instead /etc/os-release contains a non-UTF-8 byte, UnicodeDecodeError escapes run() and the process exits with a traceback (permanently dead in the default nohup provisioning mode).
fix: Read defensively: `open("/etc/os-release", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` and broaden the guard to `except (OSError, ValueError): return platform.release()`.

title: Three of OSAdapter's five abstract methods have zero callers, and the dead package_install has already diverged from the real implementation
refutation_attempt: Grepped every name across packages/ and tests/: resolve_path, package_install and os_type appear only as definitions, docstring prose, and unit-test assertions (test_agent.py:396-437) — no production caller. The divergence is real: nexus_steps/package/install.py:77 has ["sudo","apt-get","install","-y"] while linux.py:50 returns "apt-get install -y" with a Note saying the missing sudo is deliberate. It is actually worse than reported — shell_command() and temp_dir(), the two methods the auditor calls live, are consumed only at executor.py:374-375 inside _run_subprocess, which no shipped step reaches, so the entire adapter layer has zero live consumers today. What I do refute is the framing: the stated "failure" is a maintainer-confusion narrative, not a runtime defect; the methods are pinned as intended by passing tests, so nothing misbehaves at runtime.
corrected_summary: package_install(), resolve_path() and os_type() have no production callers (only unit-test assertions), and package_install() duplicates — and has already diverged from — the authoritative table in nexus_steps/package/install.py:77 (sudo present there, deliberately absent in linux.py:50). In fact the whole adapter layer is currently inert, since its only live entry point (shell_command/temp_dir via _run_subprocess) is unreachable from every shipped step. No runtime failure results; this is dead abstraction plus a contradictory second source of truth.
failure_scenario: No runtime failure exists. The realistic cost is a wrong fix: a maintainer adds the missing sudo to LinuxAdapter.package_install() (or fixes WindowsAdapter.resolve_path()'s separator handling) and ships it believing package_install steps changed, while the step keeps building its command from _INSTALL_COMMANDS in nexus_steps/package/install.py:77 and nothing about runtime behaviour changes.
fix: Delete package_install(), resolve_path() and os_type() from OSAdapter and the three subclasses (keeping nexus_steps as the single source of truth for package managers), and correct base.py's module docstring, which claims the executor uses the adapter to "run commands, install packages, and resolve paths" when only shell_command()/temp_dir() were ever wired — and even those are currently unreachable.

title: executor.py imports signal and tempfile but never uses them
refutation_attempt: Verified the imports at lines 36-37 and grepped the module: the only other occurrences of the strings are prose ("a version-skew signal" at 136, "is signalled" at 338); neither module is referenced, while `os` (line 35) is used at 378. Also confirmed ruff would already catch this: pyproject's [tool.ruff] sets no `select`, so the default E4/E7/E9/F rule set applies and F401 covers both lines. What I refute is the failure scenario — the "maintainer adds os.killpg without start_new_session and kills the agent" story is speculative, not a defect in the code as written; no runtime behaviour is affected.
corrected_summary: `import signal` (line 36) and `import tempfile` (line 37) are unused anywhere in the 669-line module — a lint violation that ruff's default F401 rule would flag. The signal import is mildly misleading next to the AI Note at 338-341 explaining that no process-group signalling exists, but nothing misbehaves at runtime.
failure_scenario: No runtime failure. `ruff check packages/agent` reports two F401 violations on executor.py:36-37, so the module fails a clean lint run; the risk beyond that is only reader confusion about whether signal-based escalation already exists.

title: _CAP_BYTES truncation counts characters, not bytes, so non-ASCII output overshoots the cap
refutation_attempt: Code reads as described: _CAP_BYTES = 256*1024 is documented as a "Per-stream byte cap" (461-467) but `len(text)` and `text[-self._CAP_BYTES:]` operate on str code points. The path is reachable for shipped steps via the temp-file branch (poll steps set stdout_path, and _read does f.read() then truncates). test_capture_truncates_oversized_stream (test_agent.py:1123) uses ASCII, so it does not pin character semantics as intended. I did refute the severity, though: uvicorn's ws_max_size defaults to 16 MiB (uvicorn/config.py:189) and the server sets no override, so a ~2 MB frame is accepted rather than rejected — there is no lost step result, only an oversized frame and a bloated Job.log_text row. The marker prefix also means the cap is already exceeded slightly by design.
corrected_summary: The cap advertised as a per-stream byte cap is enforced on characters, so UTF-8 output can exceed it by up to 4x (e.g. 256k CJK characters ≈ 768 KB). Impact is bounded to bloat — frames up to ~2 MB and correspondingly large Job.log_text rows — not delivery failure, since uvicorn accepts WebSocket messages up to 16 MiB by default.
failure_scenario: A run_command step whose output is CJK or emoji-heavy (non-Latin locale test output, a Unicode progress UI) writes 256,000 characters to its stdout temp file. _capture sees len == 256,000 <= 262,144 and skips truncation, so ~768 KB of stdout plus a similar stderr go into one StepCompleted frame and into Job.log_text — roughly 3x the size the docstring at 462-467 says the cap guarantees.
fix: Cap on the encoded length: `raw = text.encode("utf-8"); if len(raw) > self._CAP_BYTES: text = "…[truncated]…\n" + raw[-self._CAP_BYTES:].decode("utf-8", errors="ignore")`.

title: AgentConfig.load()'s node_id fallback diverges from its two sibling code paths
refutation_attempt: The divergence is real (line 69, 149 and 200 all carry `platform.node() or f"node-{uuid4().hex[:8]}"`; line 212 does not), and test_node_id_defaults_to_platform_node_or_random (test_agent.py:80-90) states the intended invariant that node_id is always a non-empty string, so load() breaking it is a genuine inconsistency. But I refuted most of the impact. Reachability: the only writer of config.json is `nexus-agent init` via create() (provisioner.py:159), which always persists a non-empty string, so a null node_id requires a hand-edited or hand-templated file. And the empty-string variant is harmless: the WS route is /ws/agent/{node_id} (ws.py:252) so the server takes the node id from the URL path and ignores the register/heartbeat node_id field entirely (ws.py:409-419 passes the path node_id to update_node), making the extra `&node_id=` query parameter and the register field cosmetic — contrary to both the auditor's and the test docstring's "unroutable registration" claim.
corrected_summary: load()'s file branch uses bare `data.get("node_id", platform.node())`, dropping the uuid fallback and None guard that the dataclass default_factory (69), create() (149) and load()'s CLI branch (200) all have. An explicitly null node_id in a hand-written config therefore yields node_id=None and a pydantic ValidationError at registration that escapes run() and kills the process; the empty-hostname variant is cosmetic only, since the server derives the node id from the URL path.
failure_scenario: A provisioning template (or hand edit) writes `"node_id": null` into config.json. The explicit None suppresses the default_factory, _send_registration() builds AgentRegister(node_id=None), pydantic raises ValidationError, and because ValidationError is not in run()'s transient tuple the nexus-agent process exits with a traceback on every start rather than falling back to a generated id.
fix: Make line 212 match its siblings: `node_id=node_id or data.get("node_id") or platform.node() or f"node-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"`.

refutation_attempt: Found directly by the adversarial verifier while re-reading the code.
title: detect_capabilities() runs up to ~25s of blocking host probes inline on the event loop on every reconnect
corrected_summary: _send_registration() calls the synchronous detect_capabilities() directly from a coroutine, so its subprocess probes — nvidia-smi (10s timeout), system_profiler (10s), sysctl (5s), documented at capability.py:52-54 as "roughly 25s if every probe hits its timeout" — block the agent's single event loop on every connect and reconnect. Neither docstring mentions the event-loop impact.
failure_scenario: A node with a wedged nvidia-smi (a common GPU-driver fault leaves it unkillable in D-state) reconnects after a server restart. detect_capabilities() blocks the loop for the full 10s timeout at connection.py:317 before the register frame is even built: during that window no heartbeat is sent, no inbound execute_step frame is read, every running poll step's 1s check() tick is skipped, and any step.completed waiting in send_message's retry loop is delayed. Since this runs on every reconnect, a flapping link multiplies the stall.
fix: `caps = await asyncio.to_thread(detect_capabilities)` at connection.py:317 — the probes are already self-timeboxed, so a thread is the minimal change and keeps the loop responsive during registration.

title: ContextSatisfiableRule's documented pattern cannot actually be used with a required schema field: pass 3 always rejects the seeded None
refutation_attempt: I reproduced all the cases. Required `str` field + ContextSatisfiableRule("binary_path", "build_output") with ctx {'build_output': None} -> ['_schema: ... binary_path Field required']; with a *real* value {'build_output': '/tmp/x'} it ALSO fails the same way, because ctx.resolve merges by key name only — so the differing-context_key form of the rule is broken even at runtime, which is worse than the auditor stated (an Optional field would pass validation but receive None, silently). With context_key == field_name and a None placeholder: ['_schema: ... Input should be a valid string [input_value=None]']; with a real same-named value: clean. I then checked what refutes the auditor's framing: the optional-field requirement IS documented outside collect_results.py — tests/unit/test_steps/test_base.py:472-514 states in both a comment and the docstring that "the realistic shape is an OPTIONAL schema field (so Pydantic doesn't independently require it) whose presence the rule enforces", and base.py:513-519 plus jobs.py:248-252 both acknowledge the None-placeholder constraint. I also verified no shipped step is broken by this: the only user is gem5_collect_results, which uses ContextSatisfiableRule("m5out_path", "m5out_path") on an all-optional params model, and the real 2-step gem5 chain validates clean. So this is a step-author footgun and a docstring gap, not a live user-facing failure — severity low, not medium.
corrected_summary: ContextSatisfiableRule's docstring (base.py:230-241) advertises "required UNLESS an upstream step provided it" and that the context key may differ from the param name, but pass 3 re-validates ctx.resolve(params) against PARAMS_SCHEMA (base.py:521), and resolve merges strictly by key name. Consequences: (a) a non-Optional field always fails pass 3 when satisfied only by context — "Field required" for a differently-named key, "Input should be a valid string" for a same-named None placeholder; (b) when context_key != field_name the value is never wired into the param at all, so even the Optional workaround hands the step None at runtime. No shipped step hits either case.
failure_scenario: A step author follows the docstring: `class P(BaseModel): binary_path: str` plus input_rules() -> [ContextSatisfiableRule("binary_path", "build_output")]. Any job pairing it with an upstream step that exports build_output is rejected with HTTP 400 `_schema: 1 validation error for P / binary_path / Field required` — verified in-process for both the None placeholder and a real "/tmp/x" value — and the message names neither the rule nor the upstream key. If the author instead makes the field Optional to get past validation, the step runs with binary_path=None because resolve() never renames build_output.
fix: Either drop None-valued context entries and treat rule-satisfied fields as absent before the pass-3 merge (base.py:521), or have ContextSatisfiableRule actually alias context_key -> field_name in resolve so the differing-name form works. At minimum state in the rule's docstring (base.py:230-241) what test_base.py:478-484 already says: the PARAMS_SCHEMA field must be Optional with a default.

title: The `-> $captures` DSL clause is dead: parser emits `_captures` and StepConfig silently drops it
refutation_attempt: Verified the mechanism: StepConfig has no model_config (default extra="ignore"), and StepConfig(**{'step':'git_clone','params':{'url':'x'},'_captures':['clone_dir']}).model_dump() has no _captures key with hasattr False. grep for 'captures' shows producers only in parser.py (361, 380-383, 389-420) and consumers only in the two parser test modules. But I refuted the auditor's failure scenario: nothing in the repo submits parser output. grep for parse_nexus_string across packages/, frontend/src and nexus_deploy.py finds only a prose mention in packages/cli/src/nexus_cli/__init__.py:17, whose own docstring says nexus_cli.main "does not exist in this tree" and the CLI is "scaffolded but unimplemented"; there is no server route that accepts .nexus text. So no user can currently write a .nexus file and have it submitted, and the impact today is dead code plus a DSL that advertises an inert feature — not a wrong job. Severity low, not medium.
corrected_summary: parser.py:383 records step_record["_captures"] for the documented `-> $a, $b` clause, and StepConfig (extra="ignore") discards it on validation; nothing outside parser.py and its tests ever reads it. The grammar, _split_trailing's capture branch and ~8 tests are therefore inert. Impact is limited to dead code and DSL documentation drift, because no shipped code path submits parser output at all (the CLI that would is unimplemented — packages/cli/src/nexus_cli/__init__.py:23-26).
failure_scenario: If the CLI is completed as documented, `git_clone("repo_url": "https://x/y.git") -> $clone_path` followed by `run_command("command": "cd ${clone_path} && make")` parses cleanly, _captures is dropped by StepConfig (verified), nothing binds clone_path, and — combined with the missing ${} substitution — the second step runs `cd && make` in $HOME. Today the same file simply cannot be submitted by anything in the tree.
fix: Either implement it (add a real `captures: list[str] = []` field to StepConfig and have the runner alias step N's OUTPUT_KEYS to the capture names, since extra keys are dropped), or delete _captures, _split_trailing's capture branch and the arrow from the grammar in parser.py:15-21 so the DSL stops advertising it.

title: RequiredRule and AtLeastOneRule treat an explicit `null` as "present", replacing the friendly field error with a raw Pydantic dump under the pseudo-field `_schema`
refutation_attempt: Reproduced exactly: RunCommandStep.validate_params({'command': None}) returns a single error, ['_schema: 1 validation error for RunCommandParams\ncommand\n  Field required [type=missing, input_value={}, ...]'], with no 'command' FieldError, and StepContext().resolve({'command': None}) == {} confirms the None is stripped before pass 3 so the reported input_value is the empty merged dict. base.py:197 tests `not in params` and base.py:294-295 builds `combined = {**context.outputs, **params}` and tests membership — neither inspects the value, as claimed. What I did find that limits reach: the JobBuilder cannot produce this. buildDefaultParams (JobBuilder.tsx:187-199) seeds "" or false, never null, and handleSubmit (JobBuilder.tsx:893-896) filters out '' / null / undefined before POSTing. So the only routes are a hand-written API call or a .nexus body with a JSON null. Outcome is a correct 400 with a misleading message — low severity, matching the auditor.
corrected_summary: RequiredRule (base.py:197) and AtLeastOneRule (base.py:294-295) test only key membership, so an explicit JSON null satisfies pass 2; ctx.resolve then strips the None (base.py:107) and pass 3 reports "Field required" attributed to the pseudo-field _schema with input_value={}. The user-facing 400 (FieldError strings are user-facing per base.py:118-121) names neither the field nor anything the caller actually submitted. Not reachable from the JobBuilder, which strips null/'' before submitting.
failure_scenario: POST /api/jobs with {"step":"run_command","params":{"command":null}} returns 400 with detail `Step 0 ('run_command') validation failed: _schema: 1 validation error for RunCommandParams\ncommand\n  Field required [type=missing, input_value={}, ...]` instead of `command: required` — and the displayed input_value {} matches nothing the user sent.
fix: Use `params.get(self.field_name) is not None` in RequiredRule.validate (base.py:197) and the analogous value check in AtLeastOneRule (base.py:294-295) / ContextSatisfiableRule (base.py:255-257), so an explicit null is reported by the rule under the field's own name.

title: ContextSatisfiableRule's `context_key` is dropped by InputRuleSchema, so the UI can never explain a chained field

title: stdout/stderr temp log files are created by four steps and deleted by nothing
refutation_attempt: Looked for any cleanup owner. `grep -rn 'unlink|os.remove|rmtree|cleanup' packages/agent/src/nexus_agent/*.py packages/server/src/nexus_server/runner/*.py` returns only two doc-comment hits and no filesystem deletion; executor.py's `finally` (275-280) only pops _running_steps, and _capture()'s _read (executor.py:501-532) opens the files read-only. Verified the four creation sites by reading them (run_command.py:147-152, run_script.py:141-146, python/run.py:232-237, run_simulation.py:257-262 — all delete=False). Confirmed on disk: after a full startup/check/cancel cycle /var/folders/.../T/nexus_stdout__e9o5lli.log still existed. Tried to argue OS tmp reaping mitigates it: macOS only reaps /var/folders files untouched for 3 days and Linux tmpfiles.d defaults vary, so growth is real but slow. Severity stays low — the files are mode 0600 (tempfile default) so this is disk/inode growth plus out-of-policy retention readable only by the agent user, not a disclosure.
corrected_summary: run_command, run_script, run_python and gem5_run_simulation each create two NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) log files per execution and nothing ever unlinks them — not the step, not StepExecutor, not the runner. The leak set is actually larger than the auditor stated: gem5_run_simulation's direct-mode `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="nexus_m5out_")` (run_simulation.py:246) leaks an entire directory of simulation output, and run_python's inline-code temp .py leaks on the cancel and ChildProcessError paths (its unlink at python/run.py:324-329 is only on the reaped-cleanly path, as its own AI Note at :318-323 says).
failure_scenario: A node running 200 shell steps a day accumulates 400 undeleted files/day in /tmp (or /var/folders on macOS), plus one m5out_* directory per direct-mode gem5 run. On a long-lived lab node this is unbounded inode/disk growth and indefinite retention of job stdout/stderr outside any retention policy; OS tmp reaping does not reach recently-touched files on a busy node.
fix: Unlink state["stdout_path"]/state["stderr_path"] in StepExecutor.execute()'s finally block, after _capture() has already read them (executor.py:275-280) — one change covering all four steps. Handle the gem5 m5out directory separately, since gem5_collect_results deliberately leaves it in place (collect_results.py:296-299).

title: Store fetch() rejection leaves isLoading stuck true -> Nodes and Credentials render a permanent spinner with an unhandled rejection
refutation_attempt: I verified the store code (stores/index.ts:140-144 nodes, 301-305 credentials): `set({isLoading:true})`, bare `await`, no try/catch — so a rejection skips the second `set`. I verified no caller catches: Nodes.tsx:1247-1249 and 1254-1256, Admin.tsx:951-954 (the sibling `api.listCredentialTypes()` on 953 IS `.catch()`ed, `fetch()` on 952 is not). I looked for an upstream rescue (an error boundary, a global unhandledrejection handler, a wrapper in useWebSocket/Layout) and found none. The auditor is wrong on one point: this is NOT unflagged for Nodes — stores/index.ts:22-24 documents it, and stores/index.test.ts:236-242 explicitly pins `fetch rejects (and leaves isLoading stuck true) when the api throws` as current behaviour, so it is author-flagged at the store level (only the missing page-level `.catch()` is unpinned). Severity is also overstated: when GET /api/nodes is 500ing, the page could not show data anyway, so the actual loss is the error message plus a spinner that a reload does not fix while the server is down — no wrong action, no data loss.
corrected_summary: `useNodesStore.fetch` / `useCredentialsStore.fetch` set `isLoading: true` and then `await` with no try/finally, and no page `.catch()`es them, so a failed list GET yields an indefinite spinner plus an unhandled promise rejection — including on the un-awaited post-mutation refresh paths (`refreshAndReselect`, `onCreated`, `onAdded`). Documented at stores/index.ts:22-24 and pinned by stores/index.test.ts:236-242.
failure_scenario: GET /api/nodes returns 500. stores/index.ts:141 sets `isLoading:true`, `api.listNodes()` throws, line 143 never runs, so NodesPage:1316-1319 renders the spinner branch forever with no error and no retry, and the un-caught promise from Nodes.tsx:1248 surfaces as "Uncaught (in promise)". Same shape for the Credentials tab via Admin.tsx:952, and for the post-delete path where Nodes.tsx:609 calls `onRefresh()` un-awaited before `onClose()`.
fix: Fix it once inside each store: `try { ... } catch (e) { set({error: String(e)}) } finally { set({isLoading:false}) }`, add an `error` field, and render error+retry in the pages. That is 7 store edits versus ~11 call sites, and it makes the documented "pages are expected to .catch() themselves" contract unnecessary.

title: Maintenance button is shown to every authenticated user but the endpoint is admin-only -> guaranteed silent 403 for non-admins
refutation_attempt: Line numbers check out: Nodes.tsx:729-741 is the ungated button, sandwiched between `{isAdmin && node.status === "offline" && ...}` (718) and `{isAdmin && ...}` (743); nodes.py:552 takes `admin: AdminUser` and tests/integration/test_nodes_routes.py:375-380 asserts 403 for a regular user. I tried to refute it as intended behaviour, and it is partly that: the docstring at Nodes.tsx:542-544 states the visibility explicitly, the AI Note at 546-548 says buttons are affordances rather than authorisation, and Nodes.test.tsx:595 asserts a non-admin sees the button (though only incidentally, to prove the panel opened). I also checked the ordering question — for a non-admin the AdminUser dependency raises 403 during dependency resolution, so they get 403 rather than the 422 from finding 1. So the claim is factually right, but this is a deliberate, documented and test-pinned UI choice whose only consequence is a dead control (the server is the real boundary), which makes the auditor's "medium" too high. Note it is currently moot: the request 422s for admins too.
corrected_summary: Unlike "Bring Online" (718) and "Delete Node" (743), the Enable/Disable Maintenance button carries no `isAdmin` gate even though PUT /api/nodes/{id}/maintenance requires admin, so for `user`/`manager` roles it is a permanently dead control whose 403 is swallowed to console. Documented as intentional at Nodes.tsx:542-544 and incidentally pinned by Nodes.test.tsx:595, so this is an inconsistency in the page's own gating convention, not a security hole.
failure_scenario: A `user`-role operator opens a node panel and clicks "Enable Maintenance" to take a flaky machine out of rotation. The server returns 403 (test_maintenance_requires_admin). Nodes.tsx:590 console.errors, `onRefresh()` is skipped, the spinner flashes, the label never changes, and the operator has no way to learn the action is not available to them.
fix: Either wrap the button in `{isAdmin && ...}` (and update the docstring at 542-544 plus Nodes.test.tsx:595, which would need a different panel-rendered assertion), or keep it visible and render the caught error so a 403 is legible. Do the latter only if maintenance is meant to become non-admin server-side.

title: Credential delete swallows its error behind a `// handled` comment that handles nothing
refutation_attempt: Line 997 is indeed `// handled` inside `} catch { ... } finally { setDeletingId(null); }` (Admin.tsx:989-1003), and there is no error state anywhere in CredentialsTab except `formError`, which only the create dialog renders — so nothing is handled, and Admin.test.tsx:1310-1333 covers only the confirmed-success and declined-confirm paths. But the auditor's headline scenario is fabricated: I read the server side and there is NO referential check, so a 409 is impossible — credentials.py:82-87 returns 204 or 404 only, and db/ops.py `delete_credential` documents that `StorageBackend.credential_id` is left dangling on purpose ("no cascade and no enforced foreign keys"). What IS reachable: a 404 (the row was already deleted — and note credentials.py:83 uses `CurrentUser`, so any authenticated user can delete anyone's credential, making concurrent deletes realistic) or a 500. Also reachable and unmentioned: `await fetch()` sits inside the same try, so a failed refetch after a SUCCESSFUL delete is swallowed and leaves the credentials store's `isLoading` stuck true (stores/index.ts:301-305) — a permanently spinning secrets table. Severity is lower than claimed: the outcome is a confusing no-op, not lost data.
corrected_summary: `CredentialsTab.handleDelete` catches into an empty block annotated `// handled` (Admin.tsx:996-998) with no error state, no message and no distinction between "deleted" and "failed"; the misleading comment tells the next reader the path is covered. The reachable failures are 404 (already deleted) and 500 — not the 409 the auditor invented, since the server performs no referential check.
failure_scenario: Two admins have /admin open; A deletes `prod-s3`, then B clicks the trash icon on the same row. DELETE /api/credentials/{id} returns 404, `api.deleteCredential` throws, the catch discards it, `finally` clears `deletingId`, and B's table still lists `prod-s3` with no message — B re-clicks and gets the same nothing. Variant: the delete succeeds but the following `await fetch()` fails, which is also swallowed and leaves the secrets table spinning forever because the store never clears `isLoading`.
fix: Set a per-row or banner error from the catch (mirror `handleCreate` at Admin.tsx:1038-1044, which does surface `err.message`) and refetch on 404 so the phantom row disappears; at minimum replace the `// handled` comment with the truth. Move `await fetch()` out of the try (or give the store a finally) so a refetch failure cannot masquerade as a delete failure.

title: AI Note misstates the register-only sentinels: hostname/cpu_model "pending" are not read by the UI, and hostname is often not "pending" at all
refutation_attempt: I tried to show the note is right. `grep -rn '"pending"' frontend/src` (excluding tests) returns only job/step/transfer status literals plus the two write sites at Nodes.tsx:922 and 927 — nothing anywhere in frontend/src reads `hostname === "pending"` or `cpu_model === "pending"`, and on the server the string appears only in comments/docstrings (nodes.py:414-420 prose, ops/models docstrings), never in a comparison. The only register-only sentinel actually consumed is `ip_address !== "0.0.0.0"` at Nodes.tsx:351, which its own note documents correctly. Line 922 is `hostname: name.trim() || "pending"`, so typing the Display Name the label at 998 invites makes hostname the display name, not the sentinel. The note is defensible only in its final clause ("the POST body must satisfy the server's required-field validation, which is why they exist at all"), which is the actual reason. So: the note is overstated/partly false, but there is no runtime failure — the auditor's scenario is hypothetical future code, which is why this is low, not medium.
corrected_summary: The AI Note at Nodes.tsx:916-920 claims `hostname: "pending"`, `cpu_model: "pending"` and `ip_address: "0.0.0.0"` are "the sentinels the rest of the UI keys off". Verified false for two of the three: nothing in frontend/src or the server compares against either "pending" literal, and `hostname` is overwritten by the operator's Display Name at line 922. Only `ip_address === "0.0.0.0"` is actually consumed (Nodes.tsx:351). In a codebase where AI Notes are treated as contracts, this points future readers at the wrong layer.
failure_scenario: No runtime failure today; the impact is on future edits. A dev/agent reads 916-920, believes "register-only nodes have hostname === 'pending'", and adds `if (node.hostname === 'pending') showAwaitingAgentBadge()`. It never fires for any node registered with a Display Name (line 922 yields e.g. "lab-box-1"), and the reader is steered away from the one signal that would work, `cpu_model === "pending"` — which is a server-side convention (nodes.py:414-420), not a UI one.
fix: Rewrite the note to state what is true: `ip_address: "0.0.0.0"` is the only sentinel the frontend reads (Nodes.tsx:351); `cpu_model: "pending"` is the server's never-connected marker; `hostname` is a placeholder the Display Name overrides and the agent overwrites on connect; the literals exist mainly to satisfy `NodeRegistration`'s required fields.

title: Artifacts table Download link points at an endpoint that does not exist (/api/artifacts/{id}/download)
refutation_attempt: Verified JobDetail.tsx:965-971 renders `<a href={`/api/artifacts/${art.id}/download`}>`. `grep -n '@router' packages/server/src/nexus_server/api/routes/artifacts.py` returns exactly one decorator, `@router.get("")` at line 70; main.py:271 mounts it at /api/artifacts. Grepped every route module for download: only jobs.py:383 `/{job_id}/results/download` and jobs.py:469's `?download` flag exist. Checked for an SPA catch-all that would soften the 404 (grep for StaticFiles/index.html/full_path/exception_handler in main.py) — none. Then I tried hard to establish reachability and found the auditor's own caveat is decisive: `create_artifact` (ops.py:1395) is called only from StorageManager.upload_artifact (manager.py:262), and `upload_artifact` has no non-test caller anywhere in packages/ — gem5 results go to PUT /api/jobs/{id}/results and land on disk, not in an Artifact row. So `artifacts.length > 0` is never true today and the whole table (and link) is unreachable. That does not make the finding wrong, but it drops the severity from the auditor's medium to low.
corrected_summary: The artifacts table links to GET /api/artifacts/{id}/download, a route that does not exist on the server (artifacts.py registers only `GET ""`), so the link is a hard 404 rather than the 401 the adjacent AI Note predicts. Latent today: nothing in production calls StorageManager.upload_artifact, so no Artifact rows exist and the table never renders — it breaks the moment that path is wired up.
failure_scenario: Once any code path creates an Artifact row (e.g. wiring up StorageManager.upload_artifact), opening that job's detail page renders the artifacts table; clicking the download icon navigates the whole SPA away to the JSON body {"detail":"Not Found"}, losing page state and downloading nothing. The AI Note at JobDetail.tsx:959-964 then sends the next maintainer hunting a cookie/session-auth problem that does not exist.
fix: Either implement GET /api/artifacts/{id}/download server-side (mirroring jobs.download_job_results including the Bearer requirement) and switch this cell to the authenticated fetch→Blob helper used by api.downloadJobResults, or remove the Download column until the endpoint exists. Either way correct the AI Note at JobDetail.tsx:959-964.

title: STEP_CATEGORIES is stale: 8 of 13 registered steps fall into "Other" and 3 of 6 declared categories match nothing
refutation_attempt: Verified STEP_CATEGORIES at JobBuilder.tsx:120-127 (keys shell/flow/git/gem5/package/system) and categorize() at 136-139 (`stepName.split("_")[0]`). Enumerated the live registry with `.venv/bin/python` after `import nexus_steps`: docker_ensure_container, gem5_collect_results, gem5_run_simulation, git_clone, git_pull, health_check, jump, package_install, run_command, run_python, run_script, sleep, update_software. Prefixes present: docker, gem5, git, health, jump, package, run, sleep, update — so only git/gem5/package match, giving 3 real sections and 8 steps in "Other", and shell/flow/system are unreachable keys. Refuted one detail of the auditor's scenario: groupSteps (line 152-168) only creates keys for categories that actually have members, so the palette never renders an empty "Shell" heading — the user sees Git, gem5, Package, Other and finds run_command under "Other". Impact is purely palette organisation; the author's AI Note at 115-118 already flags the general drift risk.
corrected_summary: The palette category map keys on the step name's underscore prefix, but the registry uses none of the prefixes "shell", "flow" or "system", and has no key for run/docker/health/jump/sleep/update. Result: three of six declared categories are dead configuration and 8 of 13 steps — including the three most-used run_* steps — land in "Other".
failure_scenario: With the current registry the palette renders exactly four sections: Git (git_clone, git_pull), gem5 (2), Package (package_install) and Other (run_command, run_python, run_script, docker_ensure_container, health_check, jump, sleep, update_software). A user hunting for run_command has no "Shell" section to look in (the heading never renders because groupSteps only emits populated categories), so the primary steps are only findable via the search box or by scrolling "Other".
fix: Key categories off the actual registry prefixes (run → Shell, docker → Docker, jump/sleep → Flow Control, health/update → System) and delete the shell/flow/system keys — or better, publish a `category` on StepSchemaInfo so the mapping cannot drift from the registry again.

title: Storage handleAddBackend docstring contradicts the code about who clears formSubmitting
refutation_attempt: Read Storage.tsx lines 288-350 line by line. Line 317 `setFormSubmitting(true)`, line 318 opens the OUTER `try`, lines 320-326 are an INNER try/catch whose catch does setFormError + setFormSubmitting(false) + `return`, and lines 345-347 are the outer `finally { setFormSubmitting(false); }`. A `return` inside a try body always runs that try's finally, so the docstring's claim that the early return "sits before the try/finally that would otherwise do it" is factually inverted. Tried to refute via the test suite: Storage.test.tsx:819-831 asserts the button is still enabled after an unparseable config — that assertion is satisfied by the outer finally alone, so it does not pin the manual clear as load-bearing. The only thing keeping severity low is that the code behaves correctly today; the harm is purely to the next maintainer, in a codebase that treats AI Notes as the contract.
corrected_summary: The AI Note at Storage.tsx:296-299 states the JSON-parse early return sits before the try/finally and warns that any new early return must clear `formSubmitting` manually or the button stays disabled forever. The early return is in fact inside the outer try (opened line 318) whose finally (lines 345-347) already clears the flag on every exit, so the manual clear at line 324 is redundant and the documented rule is false.
failure_scenario: The documented rule already fails to describe the code: deleting `setFormSubmitting(false)` at line 324 changes nothing observable (Storage.test.tsx:830 still passes because the outer finally fires). A maintainer trusting the note either adds a redundant clear on a path where re-enabling the button is wrong, or removes the outer finally believing the manual clears cover every path — at which point the server-error and success paths leave the Create Backend button disabled forever.
fix: Rewrite the note to say the outer `finally` clears formSubmitting on every exit including the parse-error return, and either drop the redundant clear at line 324 or keep it and delete the misleading warning.

title: Storage capacity field parses with parseInt, so exponent input silently records a wrong capacity
refutation_attempt: Verified line 332 `capacity_bytes: formCapacity ? parseInt(formCapacity, 10) : null` and that the source is a bare `<input type="number">` (lines 612-618) with no min/step/pattern. Checked server-side validation: schemas.py:539/563 declare `capacity_bytes: int | None = None` with no gt/ge constraint and models.py:403 documents it as "Advisory capacity for reporting; not enforced on write" — nothing rejects 1. Checked the tests: Storage.test.tsx:775 only ever types "2048", so the case is untested. I did partially refute the auditor on two details. (1) The "1.5 → 1" half is not reachable in a real browser: type=number defaults to step=1, so 1.5 is a stepMismatch, the input is :invalid, and the form (no noValidate) blocks submission — only exponent notation like "1e12", which IS a valid floating-point number and a valid multiple of step 1, reaches parseInt. (2) The claimed "permanently red full meter for an empty backend" is wrong: CapacityBar (lines 149-153) computes pct from used_bytes/capacity_bytes, so a fresh backend with used_bytes=0 shows a green 0% bar reading "0 B / 1 B"; it only goes 100% red once used_bytes > 0.
corrected_summary: `capacity_bytes: formCapacity ? parseInt(formCapacity, 10) : null` runs on the raw value of an `<input type="number">`, which legitimately accepts scientific notation. parseInt stops at the first non-digit, so "1e12" is persisted as 1. (The decimal case the auditor also cites is blocked earlier by the input's default step=1 constraint validation.)
failure_scenario: Operator registers a 1 TB NAS and types "1e12" into "Capacity (bytes)" — the number input accepts it and native validation passes, so POST /api/storage/backends is sent with capacity_bytes = 1 and the server stores it unvalidated. The card then reads "0 B / 1 B  0%" for an empty backend, and flips to a red 100% meter as soon as a single artifact lands. Impact is display-only: capacity_bytes is advisory and not enforced on write (models.py:403).
fix: Use `Number(formCapacity)` (or `e.target.valueAsNumber`) and reject non-finite, non-integer or negative values with an inline form error before POSTing; add `min="0" step="1"` to the input, and consider a `ge=0` constraint on the server schema.

title: JobDetail ignores has_log and never calls clearLogs, both of which its documented contracts assign to this page
refutation_attempt: Verified the tabs array at JobDetail.tsx:679-686 references only `detail.has_results`; `grep -rn has_log frontend/src` returns only the type declaration (types/index.ts:185), its docstring (177) and the client.ts:312 docstring — nothing consumes it. `grep -rn clearLogs frontend/src` returns only the interface, docstring and implementation in stores/index.ts (325/334/360) plus stores/index.test.ts — no production caller. So both claims are factually right. But I substantially refuted the framing of the first half: JobDetail.test.tsx:551-556 is titled "renders the five always-present tabs" and asserts "Full Terminal Log" is present on a fixture that sets no has_log — i.e. an existing test pins the always-render behaviour as intended, so the defect is in the client.ts/types docstrings, not the page, and gating on has_log would break CI. On the second half I also checked the leak framing: stores/index.ts:337-343 already documents the buffer as unbounded with no ring buffer, and because Layout owns the socket app-wide, appendLog accumulates lines for every job regardless of what JobDetail does — so clearLogs on mount would not be a general mitigation anyway.
corrected_summary: Two documented contracts are unimplemented, but the correct fix is mostly to the docs, not the page. (1) `has_log` is documented at types/index.ts:177 and client.ts:312 as the flag the detail page uses to decide which tabs to show, yet the tabs array gates only on has_results — and JobDetail.test.tsx:551-556 explicitly pins the log tab as "always-present", so the code is intended and the docstrings are wrong. (2) `useLiveLogsStore.clearLogs` is documented at stores/index.ts:334-335 as "called when the detail page mounts/switches jobs" but has no caller anywhere in the app, leaving a never-invoked API and a docstring that describes behaviour that does not exist.
failure_scenario: Concrete today: a job whose has_log is false (e.g. a pending job with empty log_text) still advertises a "Full Terminal Log" tab that only ever renders "No terminal output captured yet.". And with the dashboard socket open, step.log lines for every job accumulate in the module-singleton logs map for the whole browser session because the documented release valve (clearLogs) is never called — the store's own "unbounded, no ring buffer" note assumes that mitigation exists.
fix: Either delete `has_log` from the JobDetail type / client docstrings (or repurpose it) so the docs match the test-pinned always-render tab, and either call `useLiveLogsStore.getState().clearLogs(id)` from the id effect at JobDetail.tsx:508-528 or delete clearLogs and correct the store docstring at stores/index.ts:334-335. A real fix for the buffer growth needs a per-key cap in appendLog, not clearLogs, since Layout feeds every job's lines in.

title: Concurrent store `fetch()` calls are last-response-wins -> jobs table shows rows that do not match the active filter
refutation_attempt: I checked every store action (lines 140-144, 173-177, 210-214, 246-250, 273-277, 301-305): all are `set({isLoading:true}); const x = await api...; set({x, isLoading:false})` with no request id, no AbortController and no in-flight guard. I then looked for a downstream guard that would hide the mismatch: Jobs.tsx does NOT filter client-side - it maps `jobs` straight into the table (lines 295-330), unlike Nodes.tsx which does filter in memory (Nodes.tsx:1280-1285). So a stale response really would render rows outside the selected status. No test covers overlapping requests. What tempers this: it needs the earlier response to land after the later one, which requires two parallel connections finishing out of order - real but not the common case, and any later fetch repairs it.
corrected_summary: No store `fetch()` sequences its responses, so two overlapping calls resolve last-response-wins; on /jobs, which renders `jobs` verbatim with no client-side filter, a slow earlier response can overwrite a newer filtered one.
failure_scenario: On /jobs switch the status filter from "running" to "failed" before the first GET returns (Jobs.tsx:163-167 refetches per filter change). If the "running" response lands after the "failed" response, useJobsStore.jobs holds the running jobs while the dropdown reads "failed" and isLoading is false; the table shows rows the user did not ask for with no error, until the next fetch. Same shape for useNodesStore.fetch (line 140), which Dashboard and Nodes both call.
fix: Keep a monotonically increasing request id (or an AbortController) per store and discard a response whose id is not the newest before calling `set`.

title: `logout()` leaves every resource store populated, violating the module's own stated contract
refutation_attempt: The code fact holds: logout (91-95) clears only the tokens and `user`, while the module docstring (lines 15-20) states user-scoped stores "should be cleared in useAuthStore.logout"; the logout test (index.test.ts:143-152) asserts only token/refresh/user, so nothing pins the current state as intended. But the auditor's concrete scenario is wrong: Jobs.tsx renders `isLoading ? spinner : ...` (lines 279-287), and the store's fetch sets isLoading=true synchronously, so user B sees a spinner - not A's rows - for the duration of the request, and on failure the spinner (not A's rows) latches. Where the claim does survive is the Dashboard: it deliberately has no loading gate ("This page renders zeros rather than a spinner while they land", Dashboard.tsx:94-96) and reads nodes/jobs/pools/backends directly (lines 130-140, 148-152), so it renders the previous user's counts and recent-jobs rows for the whole round trip and permanently if a fetch rejects. I also confirmed there is no secret leak: list_credentials (routes/credentials.py:32-36 -> ops.list_credentials, ops.py:1215-1231, "no ownership or sharing filter") already returns all credential metadata to any authenticated user, and CredentialInfo carries no secret.
corrected_summary: `logout()` clears only tokens and `user`; the six resource stores and the live-log store are module singletons that survive logout and the next login in the same tab, so the next user briefly sees the previous user's data - most visibly on the Dashboard, which has no loading gate.
failure_scenario: Shared lab workstation: user A browses /, /jobs, /admin (populating jobs/nodes/pools/backends/credentials), logs out; user B logs in in the same tab and lands on / -> the four stat cards and the Recent Jobs table render A's data until B's four GETs resolve, and permanently if any of them rejects (no catch, no error UI). useLiveLogsStore also keeps A's buffered stdout/stderr for the tab's lifetime (JobDetail clears only per-job on mount). The rows are data B is authorised to fetch anyway, so this is stale/misleading state, not a secret leak.
fix: Export a `resetAllStores()` that calls `setState` with the initial value for each store and call it from `logout()` (and give Dashboard a loading gate so a failed refetch cannot show a previous session's numbers).

title: Store `fetch()` actions have no error handling: `isLoading` latches true and stale data survives a failed refetch
refutation_attempt: Verified all six resource fetches (140, 173, 210, 246, 273, 301) lack try/catch/finally while `fetchUser` (96-107) has one, so the inconsistency is inside one file. Verified the consumer really latches: Nodes.tsx renders a spinner whenever isLoading (line 1316-1320) and its mount effect (1247-1249) does not `.catch()`, so the rejection is also an unhandled promise rejection. What tempers the finding: this is explicitly author-flagged in the module docstring (lines 22-24) AND pinned by a characterisation test, index.test.ts:236-243 ("fetch rejects (and leaves isLoading stuck true) when the api throws"), whose AI Note says a fix must update the expectation. The auditor's "only a full page reload recovers" is wrong - navigating away and back remounts the page and re-runs fetch, which clears isLoading as soon as the server answers again.
corrected_summary: Every resource store's `fetch()` sets `isLoading: true` and only clears it after a successful await, so a rejected request leaves the spinner up with no error affordance until some later fetch succeeds (plus an unhandled promise rejection in the page effect).
failure_scenario: Sit on /nodes while the server restarts -> api.listNodes() rejects -> useNodesStore.isLoading stays true and `nodes` keeps the pre-restart snapshot -> Nodes.tsx shows only a spinner with no message and no retry button for as long as the server is down; the page recovers on the next successful fetch (e.g. remounting the route), not just on reload.
fix: Wrap each fetch in try/catch/finally, always clearing `isLoading` in `finally`, and add an `error: string | null` slice pages can render with a retry; update index.test.ts:236 accordingly.

title: The four hand-rolled fetches skip the global 401 handling (and getJobLog/downloadJobResults discard `detail`)
refutation_attempt: Verified all four bespoke fetches (provisionNode 203-232, reconnectNode 242-267, getJobLog 322-330, downloadJobResults 357-372) build their own headers and have no `res.status === 401` branch, while the module docstring (line 14) advertises "Globally handle 401 by clearing the token and hard-redirecting to /login" as this module's responsibility - so the 401 half is a genuine, unpinned inconsistency. The second half of the finding does NOT survive: client.test.ts:381-389 ("throws 'HTTP <status>' when the log endpoint is not ok") pins the bare `HTTP 404` throw as the intended contract for the text endpoint, with a docstring explaining the text path has no `{detail}` to unwrap, so the discarded body is deliberate rather than a defect. I also downgraded the impact: after a failed 401 provision the operator is not durably stuck - the very next `request`-based call (e.g. the node-list refetch) clears the token and redirects.
corrected_summary: provisionNode / reconnectNode / getJobLog / downloadJobResults bypass `request`, so an expired token yields an opaque error with no token clear and no redirect, inconsistent with the module's documented global 401 policy; the auditor's second complaint (dropping the server `detail` in getJobLog/downloadJobResults) is pinned as intended by client.test.ts:381-389.
failure_scenario: An operator's access token expires while /nodes is idle; they fill in the SSH provision dialog and submit -> 401 {detail:"Not authenticated"} -> provisionNode throws Error("Not authenticated") with log: [], the token stays in localStorage and no redirect happens, so the dialog shows an unexplained auth error while the UI still looks signed in until the next request()-based call bounces them to /login.
fix: Factor the 401 branch into a shared `handleUnauthorized(res)` and call it from all four bespoke fetches (leave the `HTTP <status>` message shape for the text/blob endpoints as the tests require).

title: `StepConfig` and `submitJob` drift from the server schema: per-step targeting and `storage_target` are unreachable from the UI
refutation_attempt: Diffed both sides: server StepConfig (schemas.py:228-259) has target_node_id (257), target_pool_id (258), target_os (259); JobSubmit (262-283) has storage_target (283). FE StepConfig (types/index.ts:124-128) declares only step/params/on_fail and the submitJob parameter type (client.ts:383-389) omits storage_target. JobBuilder sends only job-level targets (JobBuilder.tsx:905-906) and there is no target_os/storage_target anywhere in it. So the drift is real against the file's own stated contract (types/index.ts:10-16). What I refute is severity/framing: nothing breaks at runtime - `request<T>` does not validate and the server's extra fields are optional with sane defaults, so this is a UI capability gap, not a wrong outcome. I also checked the whole response-type surface for the more dangerous direction of drift (a declared field the server never sends) by extracting every outbound Pydantic model's fields (UserInfo, NodeInfo, PoolInfo, JobInfo, StepRunInfo, FieldSchema, StepSchemaInfo, CredentialInfo, CredentialTypeInfo, StorageBackendInfo, TransferInfo, ArtifactInfo, TokenResponse) - all match types/index.ts exactly, so the auditor's broader "silent undefined" worry is currently unrealised.
corrected_summary: The hand-mirrored request types omit server-supported fields - StepConfig lacks target_node_id/target_pool_id/target_os and submitJob lacks storage_target - so per-step targeting and a non-default storage backend cannot be expressed from the dashboard even though the parser/CLI path supports them. No runtime failure; all *response* types are currently in sync.
failure_scenario: A job needs one step pinned to Linux while the rest use the pool default. schemas.py:259 supports StepConfig.target_os and the .nexus parser lifts it out of the step body, so the CLI can run it - but adding `target_os` to the object passed to api.submitJob is a TypeScript error against StepConfig, so the plan cannot be reproduced in the Job Builder. Likewise no UI-submitted job can choose a storage backend other than the default.
fix: Add `target_node_id?/target_pool_id?/target_os?` to StepConfig and `storage_target?` to submitJob's parameter type, then surface them in the JobBuilder - or state the omission explicitly instead of presenting the type as a faithful mirror. Longer term generate these from the OpenAPI schema.

title: `submitJob` docstring states priority semantics backwards, and priority is a no-op server-side
refutation_attempt: Checked both halves. Convention: JobSubmit documents "priority: 0=high, 1=normal, 2=low - lower number wins in the queue" (schemas.py:274, field at 282), which contradicts client.ts:381 "higher runs first among queued jobs". Inertness: `grep -rn priority packages/server/src/nexus_server/runner/` returns nothing (runner.py, scheduler.py, resume.py never read it); ops.list_jobs applies only `order_by(Job.created_at.desc())` (ops.py:898); priority appears in ops.py only as a create_job kwarg (802/837) and for storage-backend ordering (1387). So no queue ordering exists at all. The only correction: the server is self-contradictory, and ops.py:819 ("Higher means more important to the scheduler") actually AGREES with the frontend docstring - so the FE is not uniquely wrong, and the same wrong belief is duplicated in JobBuilder.tsx:97-105, whose AI Note claims "the server's scheduler orders the queue by this integer, HIGHER first" while mapping high/normal/low to 10/5/1. Since nothing reads the column, this is documentation-only today.
corrected_summary: client.ts:381 documents priority as "higher runs first", the opposite of JobSubmit's documented 0=high/1=normal/2=low convention (schemas.py:274) - and no scheduler code reads Job.priority at all, so the field is inert; the server is itself inconsistent (ops.py:819 agrees with the frontend).
failure_scenario: An operator reads this docstring (or uses the Job Builder, which sends 10/5/1 for high/normal/low per JobBuilder.tsx:101-105) and submits an urgent job expecting it to jump the queue. Today nothing happens - jobs run FIFO. If priority ordering is ever implemented per the schema's documented "lower number wins", the UI's "high" (10) silently becomes the LOWEST priority in the cluster.
fix: Pick one convention, fix the losing docstrings (client.ts:381, ops.py:819 or schemas.py:274, plus JobBuilder's PRIORITY_VALUES note), state that the scheduler does not honour priority yet, and either implement the ordering in the queue query or drop the control from the UI.
